blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (and Figure 2)
blocking.issue: The pool grows by instantiating on demand while a request waits. That breaks the System overview hot-path rule that the Plugin host never instantiates. The design also cannot meet its own numbers. Creating an instance is budgeted at up to 1 ms (hypothesis), and the acquire wait is at most 1 ms (target), so growth triggered by a request rarely finishes before that request gives up with RZ-PLG-005. With only 1 warm instance per Plugin Policy, every traffic ramp or burst produces RZ-PLG-005 rejections. For closed-only auth and authz Plugins, those rejections are 401 or 403 responses to legitimate clients. Nothing bounds how many instantiation goroutines can run at once. The document also does not say what happens when `rz_configure` returns non-zero during a runtime refill, since "non-zero rejects the Revision" is impossible after activation.
blocking.evidence: Default limits table: "Grows on demand to 2 × `GOMAXPROCS` instances (target); 1 warm instance (target)" and "Wait up to 1 ms (target), then `RZ-PLG-005`". RZ-PLG table: "`RZ-PLG-008` | Instantiation failed while a pool grew at runtime". Performance model: "Instance creation from a cached compiled module | 1 ms or less (hypothesis)". Contract: "At instance creation `rz_configure` receives the Policy `config` ... non-zero rejects the Revision". System overview, Inside a Node: "Plugin host | ... | Never compiles or instantiates; an exhausted pool rejects with `RZ-PLG-<NNN>` after a brief wait". Figure 2: "alt pool exhausted or Node memory cap reached" followed by "RZ-PLG-005 or RZ-PLG-004, apply failureMode"; RZ-PLG-004 means "new instance refused", which can only reach a request if the request itself instantiates. Data plane, Plugin host: "pre-instantiated at activation and grown by a background filler; the request path takes one from a buffered channel".
blocking.fix: State that request goroutines never instantiate. A per-Node pool manager with a bounded number of workers, for example GOMAXPROCS/2 (target), creates instances in the background. It grows pools ahead of demand from a headroom target, such as keeping at least max(1, 25% of busy) instances idle (target), rather than growing on a miss. Restate RZ-PLG-008 as a background event that sets a degraded metric and never fails a request directly, and that event also covers a non-zero `rz_configure` during a refill. State whether a waiter can be served by an instance that finishes creation within its 1 ms wait.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Host Function rules; Performance model / Sizing
blocking.issue: The pool ceiling and the sizing both assume an instance is held only while the guest computes. But the one blocking State Store call runs inside a Host Function, with the guest suspended mid-call, so the instance stays held for the whole round trip. At 20,000 requests per second and a 1 ms same-zone round trip (hypothesis), that keeps about 20 instances busy per Policy, above the 2 × GOMAXPROCS ceiling (16 on an 8-core Node). During a State Store brownout at the 50 ms timeout, about 1,000 instances would be needed. A slow State Store therefore becomes Plugin pool exhaustion (RZ-PLG-005, not the STS code pack 8.6 requires) and memory-cap pressure for every Plugin that uses `state.*`, before the State Store timeout or the pack 8.7 breaker ("an open State client breaker skips calls entirely") can decide. The claim that pools stay small is false for exactly the Plugins that call the State Store.
blocking.evidence: Runtime rule 6: "An instance is held for one Phase call, never across the Upstream wait". Default limits: "Host timer cancels the call context; paused while the one `state.*` call waits". Sizing: "Pools stay small because an instance is held for one call. By Little's law, at 20,000 requests per second, 3 Phase calls per request and 20 µs per call, a Node keeps about 1.2 instances busy per Policy (hypothesis)." System overview seed budget: "Same-zone State Store GCRA round trip p99 | 1 ms or less (hypothesis)"; Configuration model Gateway: "timeout: 50ms"; Failure semantics: "`STS` when its State Store call failed or timed out".
blocking.fix: Choose one model and size the pool for it. (a) Release the instance during State Store I/O. `state_get` and `state_incr` become request-and-resume calls: the guest returns a PENDING result naming the key, the host releases the instance and performs the call, then invokes an `rz_on_state_result` export on any instance, with per-request state carried in `context.use`. (b) Keep the instance held, but size the pool ceiling as call rate × (compute + `stateStoreTimeout`) for Plugins granted `state.*`, and short-circuit `state.*` with `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` before acquiring an instance while the State client breaker is open. In either case, redo the Sizing hypothesis to include State Store hold time, and add a sizing row for a `state.read` Plugin.

blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle
blocking.issue: At the Node-wide memory cap, a Plugin upgrade deadlocks. New warm pools must be reserved before the swap. Until the swap, the old pool of a changed Plugin Policy is still the active one, so it neither drains nor frees a reservation. The transient NACK is retried "as old pools drain", but that cannot happen until the swap succeeds, so the Node retries until it is quarantined as lagging. Plugin Rollouts therefore stall under load, which is exactly when the cap binds. After the swap, up to K = 2 retired snapshots keep their own pools. Because acquisition is per Phase, those pools must still create instances for later Phases of pinned requests (`onUpstreamResponseHeaders`, `onChunk`, `onLog`), even after "old instances close when idle". So three generations of pools compete for one cap, and the document never budgets this. Separately, a Revision whose warm minimums alone exceed the cap fails on every Node, every time. That failure is deterministic, not transient, and could be computed at validation time.
blocking.evidence: Step 4: "Each Plugin Policy whose digest, `config` or limits changed gets a new pool with its warm minimum configured". Step 6: "Old instances close when idle, freeing their reservation." (after step 5, Swap). Step 7: "the retired-snapshot limit K = 2 (target)". Paragraph after the steps: "a memory cap that cannot fit new warm instances yields a transient NACK, retried as old pools drain". System overview Configuration lifecycle: "A transient NACK is retried with backoff, then the Node is quarantined as lagging". Data plane: "A retired snapshot, with the pools and Plugin instances only it uses, is freed when its pinned-request count reaches zero".
blocking.fix: Add a headroom rule. Before warming, shrink the idle instances of the pools being replaced to their busy count. Reserve a new pool's warm minimum from a swap headroom, for example 10% of `maxPluginMemoryBytes` (target), which steady-state growth may not use. If that is still not enough, swap with a warm minimum of 0 rather than NACK. State how retired-snapshot pools are sized: at most their pinned-request demand, with no warm minimum. Make "the sum over Plugin Policies of (warm minimum × `limits.memoryBytes`) is greater than `maxPluginMemoryBytes`" a deterministic validation error, with a new RZ-CFG code proposed in Open questions, so it fails a canary at once or fails in CI.

blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits; Performance model / Sizing
blocking.issue: The default 1 GiB Node cap contradicts the document's own sizing and cannot hold a moderate Bundle. Pools are per Plugin Policy, and each Policy keeps 1 warm 16 MiB instance, so 65 or more Plugin Policies at default limits cannot all be warmed. One Plugin configured per Route across 100 Routes is enough to hit this. The document's own modest scenario (20 Policies × 4 busy instances) already exceeds the cap, and the text leaves that unresolved. The default therefore produces RZ-PLG-004 or NACKs under normal use.
blocking.evidence: Default limits: "Node-wide Plugin memory (Gateway `limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes`) | 1 GiB (target)"; "with the defaults, at most 64 instances of 16 MiB exist per Node (target)". Sizing: "Guest memory is the other cost: 20 Plugin Policies with 4 busy instances each at 16 MiB reserve 1.25 GiB (hypothesis), above the default cap." Runtime rule 3: "each Plugin Policy has a bounded pool".
blocking.fix: Either key pools by (Plugin digest, canonical `config` digest, limits), so Policies that share a configuration share a pool, or give Policies beyond the first N per Plugin a warm minimum of 0. Then derive the default cap from a stated reference Bundle, for example 20 Plugin Policies at 4 busy instances plus swap headroom, which gives 2 GiB (target), or define the default relative to container memory. Keep the Sizing paragraph consistent with the default. Add a `ruralz bundle audit` finding when the static warm reservation exceeds a set share of the cap.

blocking.section: Runtime / wazero on every Node
blocking.issue: One wazero runtime per Node cannot enforce per-Plugin memory limits. wazero sets the page limit on `RuntimeConfig` (`WithMemoryLimitPages`), so the limit applies to every module in that runtime. Meanwhile `limits.memoryBytes` differs per Plugin: the default is 16 MiB and values go up to 256 MiB. Compiled code is also bound to the runtime that compiled it. So "compile once per digest" and "one runtime" cannot both hold once two Plugins, or two versions of one Plugin, declare different limits.
blocking.evidence: "Each Node runs one wazero runtime in compiler mode"; rule 4: "The page limit comes from `limits.memoryBytes`, rounded up to 64 KiB pages (target)"; Default limits: "Proposed schema maximum 256 MiB (target)". Research go-libraries-runtime.md 2.2: "`RuntimeConfig.WithMemoryLimitPages(n)` caps each memory in 64 KiB pages" (https://github.com/wazero/wazero/blob/main/config.go).
blocking.fix: Specify the mechanism. Option (a): run one runtime per distinct `limits.memoryBytes` value, share one `CompilationCache` across them, and key compiled code by (digest, memory limit). Option (b): run one runtime at the schema maximum with a host-supplied `experimental.MemoryAllocator` that enforces each instance's own cap and does the reservation accounting (https://github.com/wazero/wazero/blob/main/experimental/memory.go). Option (b) relies on an experimental API, so record that in Open questions. Update rule 1 (compile once) to match whichever option is chosen.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract and Host Function table
blocking.issue: The return convention makes `state_incr` ambiguous. Negative return values are reserved for error codes, but `state_incr` returns the counter value as an i64 and accepts a signed `delta`. A decrement, or any counter that goes below zero, is then indistinguishable from `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` or `ERR_BUDGET`. The ABI is frozen at M2, so this defect would be permanent.
blocking.evidence: Contract: "Return values | Non-negative is a length or success; negative is an error (`ERR_ABSENT`, `ERR_TOO_SMALL`, `ERR_PHASE`, `ERR_BUDGET`, `ERR_LIMIT`, `ERR_UNAVAILABLE`)". Host Function table: "`state_incr` | `(key p, l, delta i64, ttlMillis i64) -> i64`". Contract: "It is frozen when the Plugin system ships, Planned (M2)".
blocking.fix: Change the signature to `state_incr(key p, l, delta i64, ttlMillis i64, out ptr i32) -> i32`: the function returns a status and writes the i64 counter to guest memory at `out`. Apply the same rule to every value-returning Host Function. Alternatively, restrict `delta` to non-negative values, saturate the counter at zero, and document both rules.

blocking.section: proxy-wasm stance
blocking.issue: As written, the adapter cannot run real proxy-wasm filters. proxy-wasm creates a per-stream context in the guest (`proxy_on_context_create`) and routes every later callback for that stream to the same VM by `context_id`. SDKs keep each stream's HttpContext object in guest memory. Ruralz hands out an instance per Phase call from a pool, so response callbacks can land on a different instance from the one that holds the request-side state. The adapter table nevertheless says the same pools apply unchanged.
blocking.evidence: Runtime rule 6: "An instance is held for one Phase call, never across the Upstream wait; per-request state between Phases lives on the host (`context.use`)." Adapter table: "Mapping | proxy-wasm HTTP request callbacks map to `onRequestHeaders` and `onRequestBody`; its response callbacks map to `onUpstreamResponseHeaders` and `onUpstreamResponseBody`" and "Limits | The same default limits, pools, `RZ-PLG` codes and `failureMode` behavior".
blocking.fix: Define an affinity model for adapter Plugins. Pin each request to one instance from `proxy_on_context_create` to `proxy_on_delete`. Let many stream contexts share that instance, serialize calls into it with a per-instance mutex, and do not hold the instance exclusively during the Upstream wait. Size pools and account memory by streams per instance, for example at most 1,000 contexts per instance (target). Add an Open question on how pinning interacts with recycling and discard-after-fault, because recycling must wait for pinned contexts to finish and a fault loses every pinned stream's state.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract (WASI row); Packaging example
blocking.issue: The WASI rules are undefined in one place and unbuildable in another. First, the contract says every Host Function is imported from `ruralz.plugin.v1`, that every Host Function requires exactly one Capability, and that Capabilities are derived from imports. But WASI imports come from `wasi_snapshot_preview1`, and the document never says how they map to Capabilities or whether they count in the subset check. Second, making every environment call fail breaks toolchains that read args and environ at start-up. Go's wasip1 runtime aborts when `environ_sizes_get` returns an error. Go and TinyGo runtimes also import `clock_time_get` and `random_get` unconditionally, so the scaffolded Go/TinyGo PDK (M2) would need `clock.read` and `random.read`. The canonical geo-block example grants neither, so it would fail activation with RZ-CFG-028.
blocking.evidence: "Host import module | All Host Functions are imported from the module named `ruralz.plugin.v1`"; "Every Host Function requires exactly one Capability; there is no ambient authority"; "Requested Capabilities | Derived from imports, never self-declared; they MUST be a subset of `spec.capabilities`"; "WASI | A Ruralz shim only: standard output becomes `log.write`, clock and random calls need their Capabilities, and every filesystem, socket and environment call fails"; example: "capabilities: [request.headers.read, log.write]   # imports beyond these fail activation"; SDK matrix: "Go / TinyGo | TinyGo, or the standard Go toolchain ... | Scaffolded by `ruralz plugin init`".
blocking.fix: Add a WASI mapping table listing each `wasi_snapshot_preview1` import, the Capability it needs (or none) and the result the shim returns. `args_*` and `environ_*` return success with zero entries. `proc_exit` is treated as a trap. `fd_write` to fd 1 or 2 maps to `log.write`. All other `fd_*`, `path_*` and `sock_*` calls return ENOSYS or EBADF. Decide whether WASI clock and random imports count toward the import-derived Capabilities, and qualify the "exactly one Capability" rule to match. Add a conformance case proving that the Go/TinyGo scaffold from `ruralz plugin init` activates with exactly the example's `capabilities`, or change the example.

blocking.section: Runtime / rule 7 and Default limits
blocking.issue: Timeouts combined with discard-and-refill form a metastable overload loop. The default wall-clock limit is 5 ms (target). Under CPU saturation or GC assist, Go scheduling latency alone can push healthy calls past 5 ms, and loop-heavy guests run 10 to 20x slower with close-on-context-done. Every timeout destroys the instance, because wazero closes the module, and triggers a background refill that costs an instantiation plus `rz_configure`. That adds CPU load exactly when the Node is saturated, and nothing bounds the refills. For closed-only auth and authz Plugins, the loop turns into 401 or 403 responses across every Route that uses that Plugin.
blocking.evidence: Rule 7: "A trap, timeout or memory failure destroys the instance, whose memory may be inconsistent; the pool refills in the background." Default limits: "Wall-clock time per call (`limits.timeout`) | 5 ms (target)". Rule 5: close-on-context-done "costs 10 to 20x on loop-heavy guests". Research go-libraries-runtime.md 2.2: `WithCloseOnContextDone(true)` "stops guest execution ... and closes the module".
blocking.fix: Bound refill work with a per-Node refill worker limit and a per-Policy refill rate. Add a per-Plugin-Policy trip: after N consecutive RZ-PLG-002 results within a window (target), stop calling the Plugin for a cool-down period, apply `failureMode` directly and set a degraded metric. State whether `limits.timeout` counts time the goroutine spends runnable but not scheduled. Add a benchmark row for the refill rate caused by timeouts under saturation, and reference this mechanism from OQ-wasm-plugin-system-10.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract and Host Function table
blocking.issue: The ABI cannot be implemented or frozen as written, and it contradicts two dependencies on encoding. blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle / step 7; Runtime / Default limits
blocking.issue: Compiled native code is unbounded and falls outside every memory bound. The Node-wide cap counts only linear-memory reservations, yet each artifact may be 32 MiB, and compiled native code is usually several times larger than the Wasm input. Step 7 keeps "recent compiled code" cached without any count, size or eviction rule, and wazero keeps a CompiledModule in memory until that module or its runtime is closed (research 2.2). Each Plugin upgrade therefore leaves the previous digest's compiled code in the heap, and a Bundle that keeps changing Plugin digests grows Node memory without limit. Pack 8.11 describes `limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes` as a cap on aggregate Plugin memory. A large component that the cap does not count contradicts both the claim that the cap is a hard bound and the claim that the Node never crashes.
blocking.evidence: Hot-swap step 7: "Recent compiled code stays cached, so a rollback needs no fetch." Default limits: "Artifact size | 32 MiB (target)"; "Node-wide Plugin memory (Gateway `limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes`) | 1 GiB (target) | Each instance reserves its full `limits.memoryBytes` at creation"; "Reserving each instance's full limit makes the Node cap a hard bound". Research go-libraries-runtime.md 2.2: "By default compiled code lives in memory only until `Runtime.Close`". Pack 8.11: "Gateway `spec.limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes` caps aggregate Plugin memory per Node; at the cap new instances are refused ... and the Node never crashes."
blocking.fix: Keep in-memory compiled modules only for digests that the active Revision or one of the K = 2 retired snapshots references, and close every other CompiledModule at retire. A rollback then recompiles from the disk cache, which step 7 already assumes is cheap. Then choose one bound. Either count compiled-module size against `maxPluginMemoryBytes`, measured after compile, with a transient NACK when it does not fit. Or add a separate Node bound on compiled code, for example 512 MiB (target), plus an Open question on whether the pack 8.11 cap covers compiled code. Add a Performance model row for compiled size per MiB of Wasm (hypothesis).

blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle / step 2; Runtime / rule 2; Threat model
blocking.issue: The claim that nothing executes before verification is false when compiled code comes from the disk cache. Rule 2 loads compiled native code from a directory cache under `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}`, keyed on the wazero version. On a cache hit, wazero loads and runs that native code. Verifying the Wasm artifact's digest and signature does not verify the cached machine code. Anyone who can write to the cache directory can therefore run arbitrary native code inside `ruralzd`, outside the sandbox, and bypass ADR-0017 signing entirely. Data plane assigned the matching question to this document (OQ-data-plane-11, owner wasm-plugin-system). This document neither answers it nor lists cache tampering as a threat.
blocking.evidence: Hot-swap step 2: "The full digest and Sigstore signature are checked before anything executes." Runtime rule 2: "A directory cache under `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}`, keyed on the wazero version ..., makes restarts cheap". Data plane Open questions: "OQ-data-plane-11 | How is the on-disk compiled Plugin cache protected from tampering? | (a) Directory permissions (current); (b) a per-entry HMAC bound to the Plugin digest; (c) in-memory only | wasm-plugin-system | No". The Threat model table (PT-1 to PT-13) has no row for cache tampering.
blocking.fix: Answer OQ-data-plane-11 in this document, with one of two options. Option (a): keep compiled code in memory only, accepting a recompile after every restart, which the cold-compile row must then budget. Option (b): wrap the wazero cache with a per-entry HMAC bound to the Plugin digest and wazero version, keyed by a per-Node secret stored under `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}/identity/`, and discard entries that fail the check. Add Threat model row PT-14 (compiled-cache tampering) with the chosen mitigation and its residual risk. Reword step 2 to say that the artifact is verified before compilation, and that cached compiled code is trusted only under the chosen rule.

blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (Cold compilation time); Threat model / PT-9
blocking.issue: The 30 s compile limit has no enforcement mechanism, and its breach handling turns a compile bomb into repeated CPU burn on serving Nodes. The research names no cancellable compile API for wazero. A timeout can therefore only abandon the compiling goroutine, which keeps using CPU and memory. Because the breach is classified as a transient NACK, each Node retries with backoff and starts a new full compile each time, so abandoned compiles pile up. Compilation also runs on the same cores as request goroutines, and nothing bounds how many compiles run at once, so work that is off the request path still competes with it for CPU. Under `all-at-once`, every Node in the Cluster does this at the same moment. PT-9 admits that the bomb stops at canary only with `strategy: canary`, which leaves file mode and all-at-once Clusters exposed.
blocking.evidence: Default limits: "Cold compilation time | 30 s per artifact (target) | Off the request path | Config loader | Transient NACK, retried". PT-9: "Compile bomb | Size and time limits off the request path; NACK | Stops at canary only with `strategy: canary`". Research go-libraries-runtime.md 2.2 names `experimental.WithCompilationWorkers(ctx, n)` for compile parallelism and no cancellation. Pack 8.3: "A transient NACK (fetch, resource, timeout) is retried with backoff, then the Node is marked lagging and quarantined".
blocking.fix: Compile each new digest in `ruralz bundle build`, `ruralz bundle validate --online` and at Ruralz Control ingest, which already fetch the artifact, so that a compile bomb fails before any Rollout starts. On Nodes, run compiles through one bounded worker, for example one compile at a time with `WithCompilationWorkers` capped at GOMAXPROCS/4 (target). When a digest's compile exceeds the limit, record it and do not retry it for the same Revision, instead of retrying with backoff. State plainly that an overrunning compile cannot be cancelled and is abandoned, and bound the number of abandoned compiles, for example to 1 (target). Update PT-9 to match.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract; SDK matrix
blocking.issue: Capabilities derived from imports do not work for the engine-based PDKs that the SDK matrix schedules. A TypeScript PDK built on a JavaScript engine compiled to Wasm, and a .NET runtime, both link every Host Function binding into the engine binary, because script calls are resolved at run time. Every TypeScript or C# Plugin would therefore import, and so request, all 21 Capabilities. It would then either fail activation against a narrow `spec.capabilities`, such as the document's own example, or force operators to grant everything, which defeats deny-by-default and `ruralz bundle audit`. Extism's JavaScript convention handles this by generating each Plugin's imports at build time from a declared interface. This document cites the convention but does not adopt that step.

SDK matrix: "TypeScript | A JavaScript engine compiled to WASM, following the Extism JavaScript PDK convention"; "C# | .NET WebAssembly output, following the Extism .NET PDK convention". Test harness: "Capability cases | A call without the Capability fails at build and at activation". Deny-by-default: "At runtime, each Host Function also checks the Phase and call budget." (no runtime Capability check).

The final module then imports only the Host Functions of those Capabilities, and a call to any other binding fails at run time with a defined error. As defense in depth, add a runtime Capability check to every Host Function; today the text says each function checks only the Phase and the call budget. Add a conformance case proving that a TypeScript Plugin with `capabilities: [request.headers.read, log.write]` activates.

blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle
blocking.issue: Acceptance criterion 3 requires that in-flight requests survive a swap, and the document breaks that guarantee. Runtime rule 6 holds an instance for one Phase call only, so a request pinned to the old snapshot has to take an old-pool instance again for every later Phase: onUpstreamRequest, onResponse, onLog, and every onChunk of a long stream. Step 6 closes old instances as soon as they go idle. The old pool can therefore be empty while pinned requests still need it. Such a request must then either instantiate on the request path, which System overview forbids (see L3-2), or fail with RZ-PLG-005 under its failureMode. System overview (Compile before swap, step 7, and K = 2 retired snapshots) and Data plane both keep a retired snapshot's pools until no request is pinned to it.
blocking.evidence: L396: "6. **Drain.** In-flight requests stay on their starting snapshot and old pools, so none is dropped or sees two Plugin versions. Old instances close when idle, freeing their reservation." L79: "6. **Per-Phase acquisition.** An instance is held for one Phase call, never across the Upstream wait". 03-data-plane.md L352: "at zero pins the retirer closes only pools and Plugin instances no newer snapshot shares."
blocking.fix: Replace the last sentence of step 6 with: "Old pools keep their idle instances, shrinking at most to their warm minimum, until the retired snapshot's pinned-request count reaches zero or the K = 2 limit closes its streams (step 7). Only then are instances closed and their reservations freed." Add one sentence on memory: during a swap, the old warm instances and the new ones are both reserved against `limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes`. Add a test-harness row (Hot Reload case) in which a request held across a swap completes onResponse and onLog on the old Plugin version.

blocking.section: Runtime (Default limits; Failure semantics and the RZ-PLG registry)
blocking.issue: Pools "grow on demand", and RZ-PLG-008 is a per-request result for an instantiation that fails while a pool grows. Both mean a request can trigger instantiation or wait for it. System overview, a foundation document, sets the Plugin host's hot-path rule as "Never compiles or instantiates". Data plane describes a background filler. The document says neither. By its own estimate an instance takes up to 1 ms to create (hypothesis), the same as the whole pool wait, so in practice a request waits for instantiation.
blocking.evidence: L91: "Grows on demand to 2 × `GOMAXPROCS` instances (target); 1 warm instance (target) | ... | Wait up to 1 ms (target), then `RZ-PLG-005`". L114: "`RZ-PLG-008` | Instantiation failed while a pool grew at runtime". L498: "Instance creation from a cached compiled module | 1 ms or less (hypothesis)". 01-system-overview.md L154: "Plugin host | ... | Never compiles or instantiates; an exhausted pool rejects with `RZ-PLG-<NNN>` after a brief wait". 03-data-plane.md L61: "pre-instantiated at activation and grown by a background filler; the request path takes one from a buffered channel or rejects".
blocking.fix: State that pools grow only on a background filler goroutine, triggered by an occupancy watermark (for example busy at or above 75% of live instances (target)), and that a request goroutine never compiles or instantiates. A request that finds no idle instance waits up to 1 ms (target) and then gets RZ-PLG-005, or RZ-PLG-004 if the filler was refused at the Node cap. blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 (Contract; Host Function table)
blocking.issue: The ABI's return convention reads every negative value as an error code. `state_incr`, however, takes a signed delta and returns the counter's new value as an i64. A counter that goes below zero therefore cannot be told apart from ERR_ABSENT, ERR_UNAVAILABLE or ERR_BUDGET, so a PDK author cannot implement the function correctly. The asynchronous onLog form returns 0, which is also a valid counter value.

blocking.section: Performance model (Sizing)
blocking.issue: The sizing model assumes an instance is busy for about 20 µs of guest time. A Plugin that calls `state_get` or `state_incr` before commit, however, holds its instance for the whole State Store round trip. The host call blocks the guest, and the deadline timer pauses, but the instance is not released. System overview puts a same-zone round trip at up to 1 ms p99 (hypothesis). At the model's 20,000 requests per second, Little's law then gives about 20 busy instances per Policy (hypothesis), more than the 2 × GOMAXPROCS ceiling of 16 on an 8-core Node. In a State Store brownout each call holds its instance for up to `stateStoreTimeout`, 50 ms in the Configuration model example. The Plugin then fails with RZ-PLG-005 (pool exhausted), not the STS path pack 8.6 prescribes for State Store failures. Architects and operators cannot size pools or the Node memory cap from this section.
blocking.evidence: L505: "Pools stay small because an instance is held for one call. By Little's law, at 20,000 requests per second, 3 Phase calls per request and 20 µs per call, a Node keeps about 1.2 instances busy per Policy (hypothesis)." L89: "Host timer cancels the call context; paused while the one `state.*` call waits". 01-system-overview.md L262: "Same-zone State Store GCRA round trip p99 | 1 ms or less (hypothesis)". Pack 8.6: "A rejection uses `STS` when a State Store call failed or timed out".
blocking.fix: Add a State Store term to Sizing, busy instances ≈ rate × (guest time + State Store wait), with a worked example tagged (hypothesis) and the resulting memory-cap arithmetic. Then choose one remedy: (a) scale the pool ceiling of Plugins that hold `state.read` or `state.write` with `stateStoreTimeout`, and report pool exhaustion caused by an in-flight State Store wait as `RZ-STS`; or (b) state that State Store calls park the guest and release its CPU but keep the instance, and bound the number of parked instances separately.

On-demand growth and RZ-PLG-008 also contradict System overview, which says the Plugin host 'Never compiles or instantiates' on the hot path, and Data plane, which grows pools in a background filler.
blocking.evidence: L80: "A trap, timeout or memory failure destroys the instance ...; the pool refills in the background."; L91: "Grows on demand to 2 × `GOMAXPROCS` instances ... Wait up to 1 ms (target), then `RZ-PLG-005`"; L114: "`RZ-PLG-008` | Instantiation failed while a pool grew at runtime"; System overview L154: "Never compiles or instantiates".
blocking.fix: Grow and refill pools only in a background filler with a per-Policy rate limit and backoff, each tagged (target). Add a per-Policy fault breaker. Make RZ-PLG-008 a background-only event. Add a threat row for attacker-triggered faults, plus an audit finding for any enforcing Plugin (response.send, or a body or stream write Capability) set to failureMode open, and recommend closed. Tell PDKs to read bodies in chunks by offset.

blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits; Performance model / Sizing; Threat model PT-6, PT-8
blocking.issue: One Plugin Policy can take the whole first-come, first-served Node cap. Pools grow to 2 × GOMAXPROCS, only one warm instance is reserved, and instances are held through the State Store call with the timer paused. A State Store brownout or slow input therefore inflates one pool until every other Policy, including authz Plugins (403 for all traffic), gets RZ-PLG-004. The document's own sizing already exceeds the default cap.
blocking.evidence: L89: "paused while the one `state.*` call waits"; L91: "1 warm instance (target) | Also bounded by the Node-wide memory cap"; L509: "20 Plugin Policies with 4 busy instances each at 16 MiB reserve 1.25 GiB (hypothesis), above the default cap."
blocking.fix: Reserve each Policy's warm minimum at activation and cap each pool's growth at a fair share of the Node cap (target). Reserve auth- and authz-class pools first. Size the default cap from the document's own model. Warn at validation when 2 × GOMAXPROCS × memoryBytes exceeds the cap. Add a threat row.

blocking.section: Runtime (rule 4) and Default limits; Threat model PT-6
blocking.issue: The wazero page limit is set on RuntimeConfig, so it is runtime-wide, and the document runs one runtime per Node. A guest declared at 16 MiB that omits a memory maximum can grow to the largest limit in the Revision (up to 256 MiB), while the reservation counter charges only 16 MiB. The Node cap is therefore not a hard bound, and the Node can be OOM-killed, breaking P6 and pack 8.11.
blocking.evidence: L70: "Each Node runs one wazero runtime"; L77: "The page limit comes from `limits.memoryBytes`"; L99: "makes the Node cap a hard bound"; research 2.2: "`RuntimeConfig.WithMemoryLimitPages(n)` caps each memory".
blocking.fix: Name the per-Plugin mechanism: one runtime per memory limit sharing a CompilationCache; or rejecting any module whose declared memory maximum is missing or above limits.memoryBytes (RZ-CFG-028); or an experimental.MemoryAllocator that refuses to grow past the limit. Add a fuzz and conformance test that grows memory past the declared limit.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract and Host Function table
blocking.issue: The ABI does not say how the host validates what a guest writes into HTTP messages. Header set, body replace and response_send accept any name, value and status. That permits CR, LF and NUL injection, overwriting framing and hop-by-hop headers (Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Host, Connection, pseudo-headers), a Content-Length that no longer matches a replaced body, and 1xx statuses. These are classic request-smuggling and response-splitting paths, and the ABI is also the proxy-wasm and multi-protocol contract.
blocking.evidence: L148: "`request_header_set` | `(name p, l, value p, l) -> i32`"; L154: "`response_header_set`"; L157: "`response_send` | `(status i32, body p, l) -> i32`"; no validation rule appears in the ABI.
blocking.fix: Add a rule: header names are RFC 9110 tokens; values contain no CR, LF or NUL; hop-by-hop, framing and pseudo-headers and Host are read-only; the host recomputes framing after a body replacement; status is 200 to 599. A violation returns ERR_INVALID and counts toward RZ-PLG-007. Cover the rule in conformance and fuzz tests.

blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle / Canary percentage
blocking.issue: The recommended per-request canary splits traffic 'on a header', so the client chooses the Plugin version, and for an authz Plugin an attacker selects the weaker one. If the two when expressions are not exhaustive, neither Policy runs, and the control is silently skipped. Nothing validates that the pair is complementary.
blocking.evidence: L434: "two `plugin` Policies with complementary `when` expressions, for example on a header or Consumer Tier; each has its own slot, so exactly one runs."
blocking.fix: For auth and authz classes, require the split to use only authenticated attributes, never client headers (MUST). Require the pair to be written as X and !(X), with an error-level audit finding when it is not. Recommend only the Rollout canary for security classes.

blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (Cold compilation time, Artifact size); Threat model PT-9
blocking.issue: No research supports the 30 s compile bound, since nothing shows that wazero compilation honors cancellation, and Go cannot kill a goroutine. Compile memory is unbounded and sits outside maxPluginMemoryBytes. A pathological 32 MiB artifact can exhaust memory on serving Nodes, and in file mode on all of them at once. A compile timeout is classed as a transient NACK and retried, although it reproduces from the Revision, so the cost repeats and a canary does not stop it.
blocking.evidence: L97: "Cold compilation time | 30 s per artifact (target) | ... | Transient NACK, retried"; L525: "PT-9 | Compile bomb | Size and time limits off the request path; NACK".
blocking.fix: Add pre-compile structural limits (function count, code size, locals, table and data sizes), each tagged (target), checked in plugin build, at Ruralz Control ingest and on Nodes. Compile in a bounded worker with a memory ceiling. Treat a limit breach as a deterministic RZ-CFG-028 NACK. Add an Open question and a research action on wazero honoring cancellation during CompileModule.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Contract (Configuration row); Default limits; Hot-swap step 4
blocking.issue: The start function, WASI _initialize and rz_configure run with no deadline and no Host Function budget, and no rule says which Host Functions they may call. A looping rz_configure stalls Warm, so the Node cannot activate any later Revision, including a rollback that removes the Plugin. It also starves background refills.
blocking.evidence: L132: "At instance creation `rz_configure` receives the Policy `config` ...; non-zero rejects the Revision"; L394: "gets a new pool with its warm minimum configured"; the limits table has no configure row.
blocking.fix: Add an instantiate-and-configure deadline (for example 100 ms (target)) with close-on-context-done. Limit configure to log, clock, random and crypto Host Functions, with ERR_PHASE for anything else. Treat a configure timeout as a deterministic NACK. Warm each Policy separately, under its own deadline.

blocking.section: Packaging / OCI artifact and Signing; Threat model; OQ-wasm-plugin-system-6
blocking.issue: Anyone with Git write access controls the registry host in Plugin.spec.image. Ruralz Control at ingest, CI builds and every Node fetch from that host before any signature check, which is SSRF into operator networks (metadata endpoints, internal services). Registry credentials can also leak to a hostile host or through a cross-host redirect.
blocking.evidence: L328: "Nodes, Ruralz Control and the CLI fetch it with `oras-go`"; L341: "in Ruralz Control at ingest and on each Node at activation"; L343: "Registry credentials and pull fan-out are OQ-wasm-plugin-system-6."
blocking.fix: Put a registry host allowlist in the Plugin trust policy (process configuration, never a Bundle) and reject other hosts with RZ-CFG-028 before any I/O. Refuse link-local, loopback and private addresses unless explicitly allowed. Bind each credential to its exact host and never forward it across redirects. Add a threat row.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Host Function rules (Metrics); Observability; Canary percentage
blocking.issue: Guest metric names share the host's namespace. A guest metric named 'failures' becomes ruralz_plugin_failures_total, the same name as the proposed host counter with a different label set, which can break the scrape. A Plugin can therefore blind or corrupt the trap, timeout and pool signals proposed as canary gates, and so pass its own canary.
blocking.evidence: L171: "Names become `ruralz_plugin_<name>_total`, labeled only by Policy"; L485: "`ruralz_plugin_failures_total` by code"; L432: "proposes the Plugin trap, timeout and pool-exhaustion rates as gate signals".
blocking.fix: Put guest metrics in one family, ruralz_plugin_guest_total{policy,name}. Validate name as ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,62}$ and reject reserved names. Record the rule in OQ-wasm-plugin-system-12.

blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Figure 2; Packaging / example
blocking.issue: The canonical authz example decides on a country header that the client controls. Unless a trusted edge overwrites that header, an attacker sends an allowed country and bypasses the Policy. failureMode closed does not help, because the Plugin decides wrongly rather than failing. Authors will copy the pattern.
blocking.evidence: L251: "request_header_get for the country header"; L366: "capabilities: [request.headers.read, log.write]"; L381: "filterClass: authz".
blocking.fix: State that the header MUST come from a trusted edge that overwrites any client value, and point to the built-in authz.geoip (Planned (M2)). Add a threat row, 'Plugin decision on spoofable input'.

blocking.section: proxy-wasm stance / Adapter rules (Capabilities)
blocking.issue: proxy-wasm imports are multiplexed: one header-map import serves request and response headers and trailers by argument, and the property getter reads arbitrary paths. A one-import-to-one-Capability mapping derived from imports therefore over-grants, and deny-by-default does not hold for any proxy-wasm Plugin.
blocking.evidence: L540: "Each proxy-wasm import maps to a Ruralz Host Function and its Capability; the same deny-by-default rules and online check apply".
blocking.fix: Require the union of every Capability a multiplexed import can reach, or check the selector argument against spec.capabilities on every call. Map property paths through an explicit allowlist. Add this to adapter conformance and OQ-8.

blocking.section: Default limits (Instance recycling); Threat model PT-11; Sandbox layers
blocking.issue: Instances are reused across requests for up to 100,000 calls, and PT-11 accepts that a guest can retain data between calls, so request A's credentials can leak into request B through a guest bug. That contradicts Security and identity ('Instances never share memory across Plugins or requests') and this document's own Data layer claim.
blocking.evidence: L92: "After 100,000 calls (target) or any fault"; L527: "A buggy guest can retain data between calls"; L318: "No access to other requests"; Security and identity L417: "Instances never share memory across Plugins or requests."
blocking.fix: Reconcile the two documents: reword the Data layer and have Security and identity amend L417, or add a fresh-instance mode through an Open question. Require PDKs to zero buffers that held host data, and add a cross-request leakage conformance case.

blocking.section: Goals and prior art; Packaging

The research that does cover cosign records the verification-bypass advisory GHSA-fx35-mq7g-6g98, which the document ignores while it hypothesizes cosign interoperability.
blocking.evidence: L55: krakend.io/blog/dropping-plugins-support-on-community; L328: github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go; L341: github.com/sigstore/cosign. These appear only in go-libraries-protocols.md, tooling-and-licenses.md, krakend-parity.md and licensing-landscape.md.
blocking.fix: Add go-libraries-protocols.md and krakend-parity.md to the manifest research list, or re-cite URLs from the declared files. Pin cosign v3.1.3 or v2.6.5 or newer for the interoperability test.

non_blocking.suggestion: Say where the signature mode is set: in the trust policy in process configuration, never in a Bundle. Say that warn is accepted only by ruralz dev run.

Unchanged pools carry over and publisher revocation applies only at the next activation, so a Plugin from a revoked publisher keeps running. Say whether trust-policy.changed re-verifies active artifacts, and what happens when one fails.
Verify the signature before any WASM parsing. Enforce the 32 MiB limit while streaming. Require exactly one config and one layer, and cap the config blob size and the referrer count.

non_blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Host Function table
non_blocking.suggestion: Say that random_bytes uses crypto/rand. Replace 'After authentication' for consumer_info with Phase rules, and add a PII audit finding for claims. Note that Go and TinyGo runtimes need random.read and clock.read at start-up.

blocking.section: Runtime / rule 7 and Default limits (Instance pool size, Pool manager, Cold compilation); Performance model / Sizing; Capabilities and sandboxing / audit
blocking.issue: This is a new regression from the round-2 fix. Pool bounds that depend on core count break at both ends of the core range. (1) The parked bound is N minus GOMAXPROCS, with N set by memory and fixed at the default cap, and it has a hard ceiling of 32. At 16 MiB and the default 2 GiB cap, N = floor(512 MiB / 16 MiB) = 32. A 16-core Node therefore gets 16 parked slots, below the 20 that the document's own healthy `state.read` row needs at 20,000 requests per second, and a 16-core Node would normally carry more traffic than that. A Node with 32 or more cores gets 0 parked slots, so every `state_*` call returns ERR_UNAVAILABLE and yields RZ-STS, even at 1 request per second against a healthy State Store. Closed Policies then deny all traffic. The fixed ceiling of 32 also ignores throughput: a large Node at 60,000 requests per second with a 1 ms round trip needs about 60 parked slots. `ruralz bundle audit` runs offline and cannot see GOMAXPROCS, so a Plugin with N >= 32 passes the audit and still fails on large Nodes. (2) At the small end, `GOMAXPROCS`/2 pool-manager workers is 0 when GOMAXPROCS = 1, which is a common Kubernetes CPU limit. With no workers, no instance is ever created and every Plugin call fails with RZ-PLG-005. Likewise, `WithCompilationWorkers` capped at `GOMAXPROCS`/4 gives 0 below 4 cores.
blocking.evidence: Default limits: "at most min(2 × `GOMAXPROCS`, N) computing and, in `state.*` pools, max(0, min(32, N − `GOMAXPROCS`)) parked; warm minimum 1 (target)" and "Share: 25% of the Node cap (target)"; "Node Plugin memory (Gateway `limits.maxPluginMemoryBytes`) | 2 GiB (target)". Rule 7: "beyond the parked bound, or with the State client breaker open, `state_*` returns `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` at once, yielding `RZ-STS`". Sizing: "`state.read` 16 MiB, healthy | 20,000 requests/s, 20 µs plus a 1 ms round trip; N = 32, parked bound 24 on 8 cores | 20 parked (hypothesis)". Audit: "`state.*` Plugins with N below 32 (target)". Pool manager: "`GOMAXPROCS`/2 workers". Cold compilation: "`WithCompilationWorkers` at most `GOMAXPROCS`/4".
blocking.fix: Stop deriving the parked bound from GOMAXPROCS. Reserve a small number of compute slots that does not grow with cores, for example reserved = min(floor(N/4), max(2, ceil(2 × observed compute busy))) (target). Set parked = N − reserved, and either drop the fixed ceiling of 32 or scale it with call rate × `stateStoreTimeout`. The default `maxPluginMemoryBytes` is materialized into the Revision, so it cannot depend on core count. Instead, let the share for `state.*` pools grow (for example, up to 50% of the cap (target)), or state that large Nodes need a larger cap. Because the audit cannot see cores, have the Node emit a degraded metric and log line at activation when a `state.*` pool's parked bound is below a threshold. Use max(1, GOMAXPROCS/2) pool-manager workers and max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) compile workers. Add Sizing rows for the 16 MiB `state.read` Plugin on 16-core and 32-core Nodes, and correct the audit rule to match.

blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (Compiled code per Node); Failure semantics and the RZ-PLG registry
blocking.issue: The document calls the Revision-only compiled-code limit a deterministic RZ-CFG-028, but the limit is measured on native compiled code. That size depends on CPU architecture: wazero compiles to amd64 or arm64, and the two produce different code. It also depends on the wazero version, and the research names no API for measuring compiled size. The result therefore does not reproduce from the Revision, which contradicts pack 8.3's definition of a deterministic NACK and pack 8.1's rule that equal digests mean equal behavior. In a Cluster that mixes amd64 and arm64, or where CI links a different wazero, one canary Node can NACK 'deterministically' and trigger `autoRollback` for a Revision that fits on every other Node. The online stage (CI and ingest) also cannot reproduce a number measured on a Node. The round-2 non-blocking note asking how the bound is measured was not addressed, and OQ-wasm-plugin-system-16 does not cover it.
blocking.evidence: Default limits: "Compiled code per Node | 512 MiB (target) | Active and retained snapshots | RZ-CFG-028 when the Revision alone exceeds it; transient NACK while retained code blocks it". Failure semantics: "Deterministic failures reproduce from the Revision and fail the gate at once (pack section 8.3): ... size, structure or Revision-only compiled-code limits". Performance model: "Compiled code per MiB of Wasm | 4 MiB or less (hypothesis)". Pack 8.3: "A deterministic NACK is an `RZ-CFG-<NNN>` error that reproduces from the Revision; it fails the gate at once." Pack 8.1: "Equal digests mean equal effective behavior on every Node that accepts them". Research go-libraries-runtime.md 2.2: "The Compiler (AOT) mode works only on amd64 and arm64" (the research lists no compiled-size API).
blocking.fix: Make the deterministic check a function of the Revision only. For example, RZ-CFG-028 applies when the sum over distinct Plugin digests of artifact bytes × a fixed factor of 4 (matching the hypothesis row) exceeds 512 MiB, or when the Wasm bytes of the Revision alone exceed 128 MiB (target). The online stage and every Node then compute the same answer. Classify an overrun measured on a Node, however it is measured, as a transient NACK plus a degraded metric, never as RZ-CFG-028. State how a Node measures compiled size, for example as the process heap delta around each compile or as a Wasm-size estimate, and add the measurement to OQ-wasm-plugin-system-16.

non_blocking.section: Hot-swap lifecycle / step 4; Performance model / Sizing
non_blocking.suggestion: Pools are keyed per configuration, so one Plugin configured differently on many Routes owns many pools, and upgrading it replaces all of them at once. In the reference Bundle (20 pools, 1.25 GiB), a full replacement needs about 2.5 GiB before the swap, above the 2 GiB cap. About 40% of the new pools would then 'start at 0' and serve RZ-PLG-005 until the replaced pools trim after the swap. For auth and authz Plugins that means 401 or 403 responses. The sentence 'plus swap replacements and headroom' is true only for partial replacements. Qualify that sentence and state the expected rejection window (target). Add a Hot Reload test case that replaces every pool of a many-pool Plugin under load, and an audit finding when one Plugin's aggregate peak exceeds the memory free at swap time.

non_blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (Fault breaker); Threat model / PT-15
non_blocking.suggestion: The fault breaker is per pool and trips on a ratio, so it amplifies denial of service. On a low-traffic pool, about 101 crafted faulting requests in 10 s trip it, and then 95% of legitimate traffic is denied (closed) or bypassed (open) for 5 s, again and again. PT-15 accepts this, but consider tracking faults per client identity (source address or Consumer) and requiring a minimum number of distinct faulting clients before tripping. Alternatively, for closed auth and authz Plugins, keep calling the guest and rely only on the bounded refill rate.

non_blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / WASI shim table
non_blocking.suggestion: `sched_yield` still has no row, and the standard Go wasip1 runtime imports it. Returning ENOSYS from `poll_oneoff` may abort Go and TinyGo guests: the Go wasip1 runtime is understood to throw when `poll_oneoff` fails in its sleep and idle paths, though this has not been verified against the research. Name `sched_yield` (success). For `poll_oneoff`, choose either a clock-only subscription that returns at once or a trap mapped to RZ-PLG-001, so that the Go/TinyGo scaffold conformance case is deterministic.

'Full reservation makes the Node cap a hard bound on linear memory' holds only for live pages. Unless instances use `WithMemoryCapacityFromMax(true)` (research 2.2), each `memory.grow` reallocates and copies, so the old buffers stay garbage in the Go heap until the next GC. The live linear memory also raises the GC heap goal. State the allocation mode, and describe how the Plugin reservation interacts with GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT in the Data plane memory sum.

The '`state.read` reference pool ramp from 1 to 25 instances | 250 ms or less (target)' row does not match '40 at the maximum' creation throughput (hypothesis): at 40 per second, 24 instances take 600 ms. Either bound `rz_configure` more tightly for pools that need a fast ramp, or state that the ramp target assumes typical creation cost.

Because compiled code is kept in memory only and compiles run one at a time, every restart, scale-out and Zero-Downtime Upgrade recompiles the whole Bundle before `/readyz`. During a handover, both processes also hold their own Plugin reservations and compiled code. Add a boot compile-time row for the reference Bundle (target). Allow more compile workers while the Node is not yet ready. Note in Capacity planning that a handover can double Plugin memory.

With 1,000 serialized contexts on one instance, a call that runs to the 5 ms timeout blocks the other 999 streams, and the resulting discard loses all of their state. State a wait bound on the per-instance mutex (for example 1 ms, then RZ-PLG-005), and name the head-of-line case in OQ-wasm-plugin-system-17.

blocking.section: Runtime (rule 7, Failure semantics and the RZ-PLG registry), Performance model (Sizing)
blocking.issue: This is a new finding introduced with parking. When the Plugin host refuses a state_* call because the pool's parked bound is reached, the document reports RZ-STS. No State Store call was made or timed out: the refusal comes from the Plugin's own instance-pool limit. Pack section 8.6 defines STS as a State Store call that failed or timed out, and its selection rule sends Plugin limit breaches to PLG, which covers instance-pool failures. The Sizing table shows the consequence: with a healthy State Store, a 64 MiB state.* Plugin returns RZ-STS on every state_* call, so operators would investigate the State Store (owned by scalability-and-distributed-state) for a Plugin pool limit.
blocking.evidence: L73: "beyond the parked bound, or with the State client breaker open, `state_*` returns `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` at once, yielding `RZ-STS`"; L101: "A negative guest result after its State Store call returned `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` uses `RZ-STS`"; L514: "24 park, the rest get `RZ-STS` until the breaker opens"; L515: "`state.read` 64 MiB, healthy or brownout | ... parked bound 0 on 8 cores | Every `state_*` call gets `RZ-STS`". Pack 8.6: "`STS` | A State Store call failed or timed out and the Policy applied `failureMode: closed`", "`PLG` | Plugin load, trap, limit, Capability and instance-pool failures", and "A rejection uses `STS` when a State Store call failed or timed out, `PLG` when a Plugin trapped or exceeded limits".
blocking.fix: Split the two cases in rule 7. With the State client breaker open (pack 8.7 rule 2 says it skips calls), keep `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` and `RZ-STS`. Beyond the parked bound, return `ERR_LIMIT` and add a registry row `RZ-PLG-010` "Parked bound reached; State Store call not attempted". Make L101 apply only to a State Store call that was attempted and failed or timed out, or that the open breaker skipped. In Sizing, change the L514 text to "the rest get `RZ-PLG-010` until the breaker opens, then `RZ-STS`" and the L515 text to "Every `state_*` call gets `RZ-PLG-010`". Add `RZ-PLG-010` to the codes listed in the Observability paragraph.

blocking.section: Runtime (rule 7; Default limits: instance pool size); Performance model (Sizing)
blocking.issue: The parked bound falls as a Node gains cores, and at the document's own defaults it reaches zero. Parking is then refused for every call, not only under load. The bound is max(0, min(32, N − GOMAXPROCS)), and N = floor(share / limits.memoryBytes) does not depend on core count. With the default 2 GiB cap, 25% share and 16 MiB limit, N = 32, so a `state.*` pool gets 24 parked instances on 8 cores, 16 on 16 cores, 8 on 24 cores and 0 on 32 cores. Rule 7 returns ERR_UNAVAILABLE for any call beyond the parked bound. On a 32-core Node, every `state_get` and `state_incr` of a default-limit Plugin therefore fails at once with RZ-STS, even at 1 request/s with a healthy State Store. Scaling a Cluster up to larger Nodes breaks a Revision that passes on smaller ones. `ruralz plugin test` on a developer machine with GOMAXPROCS of 32 or more cannot reproduce production. The Sizing table shows the effect only for 64 MiB on 8 cores. It never states that the default 16 MiB configuration fails on large Nodes.
blocking.evidence: L73: "Every bound derives from the share, so min(`GOMAXPROCS`, N) compute slots always remain: beyond the parked bound, or with the State client breaker open, `state_*` returns `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` at once, yielding `RZ-STS`." L85: "N = floor(share / `limits.memoryBytes`) instances; at most min(2 × `GOMAXPROCS`, N) computing and, in `state.*` pools, max(0, min(32, N − `GOMAXPROCS`)) parked". L515: "`state.read` 64 MiB, healthy or brownout | Same loads; N = 8, parked bound 0 on 8 cores | Every `state_*` call gets `RZ-STS`: does not hold". L305: audit checks only "`state.*` Plugins with N below 32 (target)".
blocking.fix: Make the compute reserve a fraction of N rather than all of GOMAXPROCS, for example compute reserve = min(GOMAXPROCS, ceil(N/2)) and parked bound = min(32, N − reserve) (target). This gives 16 to 24 parked instances at N = 32 on any core count, and 4 at N = 8. Recheck the Sizing rows and add a 32-core row. State that N = 1 cannot use `state.*` and make it a `ruralz bundle audit` error. If the owner keeps a GOMAXPROCS-derived reserve, state the core-count dependence explicitly and add a Node-side transient resource NACK when a `state.*` pool's parked bound is 0, so the canary catches it.

blocking.section: Runtime (Failure semantics and the RZ-PLG registry); Plugin ABI v1 (Contract: Phase result; Host Function rules)
blocking.issue: Plugin authors cannot tell which ABI errors the guest can handle and which fail the call, and one guest outcome has no registered code. (1) RZ-PLG-006 covers wrong Phase, exhausted budget, a second State Store call and ERR_DENIED, but these are also returned to the guest as ERR_PHASE, ERR_BUDGET and ERR_DENIED. The document never says whether the host aborts the call, or whether a guest that ignores the error and returns CONTINUE is overridden to a failure. (2) A guest may return a negative value ('cannot decide'). If no State Store call returned ERR_UNAVAILABLE, no RZ code covers that rejection, yet pack 8.6 requires a code and this document owns the PLG registry.
blocking.evidence: L110: "`RZ-PLG-006` | Host Function misuse: wrong Phase, exhausted budget, second blocking State Store call, `ERR_DENIED`". L84: "1,000 Host Function calls per call (target) | `ERR_BUDGET`, `RZ-PLG-006`". L131: "negative: cannot decide, so `failureMode` applies". L101: "A negative guest result after its State Store call returned `ERR_UNAVAILABLE` uses `RZ-STS`; traps and limits use `PLG`". Pack 8.6: "A rejection uses `STS` when a State Store call failed or timed out, `PLG` when a Plugin trapped or exceeded limits, and otherwise the area of the Policy type".
blocking.fix: Add a Contract row that splits the ERR_* values into two classes. Advisory values are returned and the guest may continue: ERR_ABSENT, ERR_LIMIT on context, log and metric writes, ERR_INVALID and ERR_UNAVAILABLE. Sticky values fail the call whatever the guest returns: ERR_PHASE, ERR_BUDGET and ERR_DENIED, which yield RZ-PLG-006. Alternatively, the host traps at once on the sticky class. Register, for example, `RZ-PLG-010 | Guest returned cannot-decide` for a negative result not preceded by ERR_UNAVAILABLE, add it to the `ruralz_plugin_failures_total` codes, and add a conformance case per class.

non_blocking.section: Plugin ABI v1 / Host Function rules (State Store); Threat model PT-16
non_blocking.suggestion: The key-rate cap alone does not bound the resident key count. 10,000 keys per Policy per Node per minute, with a TTL of up to 24 h, allows about 14.4 million resident keys per Node per Policy (hypothesis), which can fill the shared State Store and evict or refuse GCRA, Quota and Token Budget keys for the whole Cell. Add a resident-key bound or a lower TTL maximum (target), and name State Store memory pressure on the Cell in PT-16.
Until the namespace component is fixed, Environments that share a State Store also share Plugin keys. Make the Environment name normative now, or mark OQ-19 'Yes, for Planned (M2)'.

Policies with the same digest, config and limits share a pool, and the breaker is per pool. An attacker who faults the guest through a public Route can therefore trip the breaker for the same Plugin's authz Policy on another Route (95% of its traffic gets 403). Keep breaker state per Policy, or share pools only within one scope and Route.

non_blocking.section: Runtime / Default limits (Instance pool size); Hot-swap step 4
non_blocking.suggestion: With a 25% share per pool, four slow or faulting pools can hold the whole Node cap. Auth and authz pools then cannot grow past their warm size (RZ-PLG-004 becomes 403). Reserve growth headroom for auth and authz pools at runtime, for example 10% of the cap (target).

'Violations are RZ-CFG-028 before any I/O' cannot hold for address refusal, which needs a DNS lookup, and a DNS answer does not reproduce from the Revision. Check every resolved address at connect time, redirects included, to defeat DNS rebinding, and classify DNS-dependent refusals as transient.
State that a rollback re-runs steps 1 to 3 (digest and signature re-checked on the cached artifact), so a tampered on-disk artifact cache cannot reach the compiler through the rollback path.

Past the parked bound, state_* returns ERR_UNAVAILABLE at once, and failureMode applies only if the guest returns a negative result. Require PDKs to surface ERR_UNAVAILABLE as a negative Phase result by default, so a PDK-built limiter that treats it as allow cannot be bypassed by an attacker who saturates the parked bound.

Ruralz Control runs guest code at ingest, inside the process that holds the Revision signing keys. Recommend running the online Plugin check in a separate unprivileged worker process, and add that to PT-1.

At activation, a Node logs a state.* pool whose guaranteed parked bound (N - ceil(N/4)) is below 16 (target) and sets ruralz_node_degraded_info{reason="plugin_parked_bound_low"} (the reason is proposed to Observability). The audit rule now flags a guaranteed parked bound below 16 and makes N below 4 an error.

L1-2: RZ-CFG-028 now depends on the Revision alone. Compiled code is counted as 4 x Wasm bytes for each distinct digest and limits.memoryBytes pair, so every stage gets the same result. A Node samples the resident-memory delta around each compile. An overrun it measures is a transient NACK with reason plugin_compiled_code_over_estimate (proposed), never RZ-CFG-028. When the open breaker skips the call, it returns ERR_UNAVAILABLE, giving RZ-STS. The failure-semantics paragraph now uses RZ-STS only for a call that was attempted and failed or timed out, or that the breaker skipped. Registry row RZ-PLG-010 is added. blocking.section: Prompt caching and semantic caching (Semantic Cache: Partitions, Storage)
blocking.issue: Semantic Cache memory in the State Store is still unbounded. (1) Only the store script prunes a partition, and only when a new entry is written to that same partition. The partition key includes Route, surface, config.key (by default the Consumer), sampling parameters, C and a digest of tools and guardrails, so most partitions are written a few times and never again. Their vector-set and sorted-set keys carry no key-level TTL, so they persist forever after the completion strings expire. (2) One store invocation may VREM any number of elements, each repairing the HNSW graph on the server's main thread, so its work has no bound. (3) OQ-18 proposes noeviction so that budget keys, which carry PEXPIRE TTLs, are never evicted. Under noeviction, growth from orphaned partitions eventually fills memory. Every write then fails with OOM, including the Token Budget reservation, whose default failureMode closed returns 503 on every budgeted AI Route in the Cell. The cache, which fails open, thus causes an outage of the Policy type that fails closed.
blocking.evidence: Line 491: "Entries are keyed by Route, surface, `AIModel`, embedding model and dimension, `config.key`, and a digest of `tools`, `tool_choice`, `response_format`, sampling parameters, C and the effective guardrail Policies." Line 493: "Vector elements carry only a timestamp; the completion is a string key with a native TTL under the same hash tag, and a time-ordered sorted set lets the store script remove expired elements and, above 10,000 per partition (target), the oldest. ... budget keys MUST never be evicted for cache entries (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-18)." Line 675: "(a) The values above, `noeviction`, in-script `VSIM` and `FT.SEARCH` (proposed)". Line 364: "`closed` rejects with 503 and an `RZ-STS` code".
blocking.fix: Under Storage, state three rules. (a) Each store sets PEXPIRE on the partition's vector-set and sorted-set keys to cache.semantic.ttl and refreshes it, so an idle partition disappears in at most one TTL. (b) One store invocation removes at most a fixed number of elements, for example 64 (target), and leaves the rest to later stores. (c) Semantic Cache memory is bounded by the store rate times the TTL (hypothesis), with a per-Node store rate cap (target) that skips stores with a counter. In OQ-18, record that noeviction makes cache growth able to fail closed Token Budgets, and ask Scalability and distributed state for either a memory ceiling with an alert or a separate deployment (option b).

blocking.section: Prompt caching and semantic caching (Semantic Cache: Look up)
blocking.issue: The lookup runs VSIM inside a Lua script to keep a hit to one round trip. Scripts forbid blocking, so a VSIM issued from Lua cannot take its background-thread path. It runs synchronously on the Redis main thread, for the full HNSW search with EF and FILTER, and it blocks every client of the deployment meanwhile, including the rate-limit, Quota and Token Budget scripts. Foundation pack section 7 and the Tech stack put vector commands on dedicated connections so that a slow search cannot delay other replies; that isolation holds only if the search runs off the main thread, so the in-script design defeats it. The per-Node concurrency cap does not help, because the Redis main thread is shared by every Node in the Cell. For valkey-search, the research never confirms that FT.SEARCH can be called from a script, and in cluster mode FT.SEARCH fans out and names no key. OQ-18 lists in-script VSIM and FT.SEARCH as proposed, yet line 487 states the mechanism as settled design.
blocking.evidence: Line 487: "**Look up** in one Lua script on dedicated connections: `VSIM` with `COUNT 1`, a bounded `EF` and a timestamp `FILTER` on Redis 8 Vector Sets ..., or `FT.SEARCH` on valkey-search ..., then read the best element's completion key." Research go-libraries-protocols.md section 8: "searches run on a background thread unless `NOTHREAD` is given". Tech stack Semantic Cache row: "Vector commands MUST NOT share auto-pipelined connections with rate-limit and quota scripts, or a slow search delays every queued reply".
blocking.fix: Replace the in-script lookup with a single threaded command per backend. On Vector Sets, VSIM ... COUNT 1 WITHATTRIBS, with the completion stored in the element's attributes, capped at a size such as 32 KiB (target); larger completions are not stored and increment the store-skipped counter. On valkey-search, FT.SEARCH ... RETURN of a completion field on the indexed hash, which uses a native key TTL and needs no sorted set. If the Lua design is kept instead, state the main-thread cost per lookup as a hypothesis bounded by EF and the element cap, and make that bound a blocking input to OQ-18. Either way, rewrite line 487 as the proposed option of OQ-18.

blocking.section: Token accounting (Authoritative usage and estimates)
blocking.issue: The estimator's cost is still unbounded when limits.maxInputTokens is not set. The Configuration model marks limits optional, and RZ-CFG-034 requires only maxOutputTokens. Without maxInputTokens the early stop never fires, and the estimator runs BPE over the whole buffered body, up to maxRequestBodyBytes (10 MiB proposed). The new per-request CPU budget has no stated action when it is exceeded: it does not say whether the request is rejected, E is truncated (which would under-reserve) or the estimator falls back. As written it is a label, not a bound.
blocking.evidence: Lines 286-288: "counts incrementally and stops with `RZ-AI-003` once the count exceeds `limits.maxInputTokens`; counts a pre-tokenized piece over 1 KiB (target) as bytes divided by 3 (hypothesis), keeping cost linear; has a per-request CPU budget (target) set by Performance budgets and benchmarking;". Configuration model AIModel sketch: "limits: {maxInputTokens: 32000, maxOutputTokens: 2048}" with no `# required` marker.
blocking.fix: Replace the CPU-budget bullet with: "after a fixed prefix, for example 256 KiB (target), or once the CPU budget is spent, counts the rest of the body as bytes divided by 3 (hypothesis), so E stays conservative and the work stays bounded". This is word-neutral.

blocking.section: Unified API (Streaming)
blocking.issue: The 1 ms p99 target for Gateway-added time to first token covers prompts of up to 4,000 tokens. It includes a strict full parse, BPE estimation of the whole prompt, and dialect translation or in-place editing. No source supports that figure for the selected library. The Tech stack row for tiktoken-go/tokenizer gives no throughput figure. The only tokenizer benchmark in the research files is for the rejected pkoukk/tiktoken-go: about 108 µs per op for o200k_base on an unspecified input. If that input is much shorter than 4,000 tokens, BPE alone could exceed the whole budget. The figure is tagged (target), but the lens requires implausible figures to be flagged, and this one cannot be confirmed.
blocking.evidence: Line 141: "Gateway-added time to first token, excluding State Store, embedding and provider time, for prompts up to 4,000 tokens: 1 ms or less at p99 (target); larger prompts add time per KiB (hypothesis)". Research go-libraries-protocols.md: "o200k_base ~108,522 ns/op against Python's ~70,198 ns/op ... (Ubuntu 22.04, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HS)". Tech stack Tokenizer row lists no throughput.
blocking.fix: Split the figure. Gateway-added time to first token, excluding State Store, embedding, provider and estimator time: 1 ms or less at p99 (target). Estimator time: a per-KiB cost (hypothesis) that the M3 benchmark measures for tiktoken-go/tokenizer. Also state that E is computed only when something consumes it: an ai.token-budget Policy, limits.maxInputTokens, strategy cost, or CEL that reads ai.estimatedInputTokens. Unbudgeted Routes then skip BPE.

non_blocking.suggestion: Say what happens when pre-content events exceed the 64 KiB hold, either commit early or treat it as a fallback-class failure, and say whether the held bytes are reserved from maxBufferedBytes. Also note that holding Anthropic ping events means the client sees nothing during long thinking. That conflicts with the 60 s idle limit between chunks (target) that Traffic management recommends for OQ-data-plane-10, so link the two.

blocking.section: Prompt caching and semantic caching / Semantic Cache (Partitions)
blocking.issue: The Semantic Cache key rules contradict the Security and identity mitigations this paragraph cites. Security and identity requires the Node to append the principal to every `ai.semantic-cache` key, and allows sharing across principals only through an opt-out field (OQ-security-and-identity-25). This document lets `config.key` fully replace the principal, so a constant key shares entries across tenants, and the only safeguard is a later `ruralz bundle audit` finding. It also refuses to cache without a Consumer, whereas Security and identity falls back to `auth.method` with `iss` and `sub`. Attack: an author writes `key: route.name`, or a copied `"shared"` example key. One tenant then sends prompts similar to another's and receives that tenant's cached completions (T13), or poisons entries that every tenant is served.
blocking.evidence: Line 491: "`config.key` defaults to `consumer.name`, as threats T10 and T13 in [Security and identity] require; without a Consumer nothing is cached unless `key` is set, and a constant `key` shares entries, which `ruralz bundle audit`, Planned (M2), reports." 08-security-and-identity.md line 353: "Ruralz appends the principal to every `cache` and `ai.semantic-cache` key ... Sharing across principals needs an opt-out field (OQ-security-and-identity-25)." T13 mitigation: "Principal in every cache key".
blocking.fix: Adopt the Security and identity rule. On Routes with an auth-class Policy, the Node always appends the principal (`consumer.name`, else `auth.method` with `iss` and `sub` or the certificate subject) to the partition, and `config.key` only adds dimensions. Sharing across principals happens only through the opt-out field of OQ-security-and-identity-25, is reported by `ruralz bundle audit`, and is treated as a `security` diff impact. blocking.section: Token accounting / Settlement; Overshoot bound
blocking.issue: The settlement table under-charges attempts that were abandoned after they reached the provider. That contradicts pack 8.9, the System overview and the Vision document, which all charge the full reservation R when usage is missing, and it opens a denial-of-wallet path. Attack: a Consumer sends prompts that make a reasoning model think for longer than `perTryTimeout` before its first visible token. Hidden reasoning tokens are never streamed, so no content event arrives, and the attempt is abandoned after the provider has already generated, and will bill, up to C reasoning tokens. Each abandoned attempt charges the Consumer only E. With retries and Provider Fallback that repeats up to (`retries.attempts` + 1) x candidates times per request, so the operator pays roughly C per attempt that no Token Budget sees. The document's own overshoot bound admits the leak ("usage billed on abandoned attempts beyond E") but picks the unsafe default.
blocking.evidence: Line 347: "| Abandoned after sending, no usage | `perTryTimeout`, pre-content stream error | E for that attempt |". Line 346: "| Error status, no usage | ... | Nothing for those attempts |". Pack 8.9: "When usage is missing (interrupted stream, no usage reported), charge all of R and emit a degraded-state metric". 01-system-overview.md line 268: "or charges the whole reservation when usage is missing". Vision line 237: "A stream reporting no usage is charged its full reservation".
blocking.fix: Until OQ-ai-llm-gateway-15 closes, apply pack 8.9 as written to every attempt that reached the provider and reported no usage. Charge the larger of E + C and any usage seen, count it in `ruralz_ai_abandoned_attempts_total`, and update the overshoot bound to match. Keep only the 'No provider attempt after reservation' release row as an OQ-15 proposal, and state that the error-status row keeps charging R unless OQ-15 amends the pack.

blocking.section: Guardrail hooks; Token accounting (estimator); Security and data residency routing (Shared provider accounts)
blocking.issue: The guardrail table promises detectors see the 'whole prompt', but much of the prompt never reaches them as text. By-reference parts (file IDs, Gemini `cachedContent`, and stored conversations) and inline media reach the provider without the Node ever seeing their text. The Node forwards them unchanged, and the estimator only counts them. Provider server tools that fetch remote content, such as web search, inject third-party text on the provider side. They are rejected only on budgeted Routes, and the document gives no per-dialect rule for recognizing them. Security and identity relies on `ai.guardrail` alone to mitigate T23 (direct and indirect prompt injection). Attack: on a guarded Route, a Consumer puts the injection or the PII in an image or a referenced file, or asks the model to search an attacker-controlled page. blocking.section: Prompt caching and semantic caching / Semantic Cache (Partitions, Storage); Open questions (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-18)
blocking.issue: The per-partition cap does not bound storage, because clients control several partition dimensions: the digest covers sampling parameters and C, which a client sets on every request. Attack: an authenticated Consumer varies `temperature` (0.70001, 0.70002, ...) or `max_tokens`, with `max_tokens` near 1, so every miss opens a new partition and the 10,000-element cap never triggers. Storage then grows at request rate x `ttl` x entry size, on the same deployment that holds Token Budgets. OQ-18's proposed option (a) is `noeviction`. When the deployment fills, every write fails, including Token Budget reservations, which default to `closed` and return 503 `RZ-STS` for every Consumer in the Cell, and GCRA, which fails open. One tenant can therefore take down AI traffic for the whole Cell.
blocking.evidence: Line 491: "a digest of `tools`, `tool_choice`, `response_format`, sampling parameters, C and the effective guardrail Policies". Line 493: "above 10,000 per partition (target), the oldest ... budget keys MUST never be evicted for cache entries (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-18)". OQ-ai-llm-gateway-18 option (a): "The values above, `noeviction`, in-script `VSIM` and `FT.SEARCH` (proposed)".
blocking.fix: Add a cap on entries and bytes per principal or `config.key` value, across all of its partitions, enforced in the store script, which skips the store and increments a counter. Quantize or bound the sampling-parameter and C dimensions of the partition. Add a memory watermark below which stores are skipped. State the storage bound as store rate x `ttl` x entry size (hypothesis). In OQ-ai-llm-gateway-18, state that under `noeviction` a full deployment is a Cell-wide Token Budget outage, and weigh option (b), a separate State Store deployment for vectors, against it.
