blocking.section: Token accounting / Settlement; Overshoot bound
blocking.issue: Partly resolved. Usage-missing attempts now pay all of R, which matches pack 8.9. The overshoot bound was not updated for per-attempt settlement, though. Admission reserves R once, but settlement charges R, or reported usage, for every attempt, and one request can make up to (`retries.attempts` + 1) x candidates attempts. A Consumer with R left in its window can therefore make the operator pay the provider for up to N x R per request, and K concurrent requests overshoot by up to K x (N - 1) x R. The only stated bound is estimate error plus hidden reasoning on `gemini` and `ollama`. Attack (denial of wallet): send prompts that make every candidate fail after the provider starts billing. Examples are a reasoning model that thinks past `perTryTimeout` with no content event, which triggers 'Timeout or stream error before content -> Provider Fallback: Yes', or an Anthropic stream that sends `message_start` usage and then an `error` event. Each fallback bills again beyond the admitted reservation. SM-10 and pack 8.9 promise a bound that this design does not keep.
blocking.evidence: Settlement: "Rows 1 and 2 apply pack 8.9, row 2 per attempt" and "| Attempt reached the provider, no usage read | ... | All of R for that attempt |"; "| Usage reported | Any attempt | That usage, summed over attempts |". Model routing: "a request makes at most (`retries.attempts` + 1) x candidates attempts (lower cap: OQ-ai-llm-gateway-16)". Overshoot bound: "a budget overshoots by at most the sum of input-estimate errors across concurrent requests (hypothesis; SM-10 ...), plus, while OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17 is open, hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama`."
blocking.fix: Extend the Overshoot bound with the term "plus up to (attempts - 1) x R per concurrent request, where attempts is at most (`retries.attempts` + 1) x candidates (hypothesis)". On Routes with `ai.token-budget`, make the safe option the default: cap total provider attempts per request at 2 (target) until OQ-ai-llm-gateway-16's attempt cap is registered, and stop Provider Fallback with `RZ-AI-005` once the attempts' summed charge reaches R. Add the per-attempt overshoot to OQ-ai-llm-gateway-15's question, because pack 8.9 and SM-10 must be amended to match.

blocking.section: Security and data residency routing / Data residency routing (last paragraph)
blocking.issue: The Semantic Cache residency rule contradicts the normative rule in Security and identity, and it permits a residency violation (T21). This document routes the embedding call and the cache entries to the serving Node's Region. It then lets a residency-split Route attach one `ai.semantic-cache` Policy per residency class, with an embedding provider in the Node's Region. Security and identity requires each embedding provider to be in the Region of the residency class its `when` selects. It also forbids any request whose class differs from the Node's Region from using the Semantic Cache. Attack or failure: operators steer clients by DNS (pack 8.13), and an EU-tagged partner hits a US Node during failover or through a misrouted resolver. The EU-class `ai.semantic-cache` Policy sends the EU prompt to the US embedding provider and stores the EU completion in the US State Store. The generation candidate stays in the EU, so the operator believes residency held.
blocking.evidence: 06 Data residency routing: "Residency routing covers only the generation provider; the embedding call, Semantic Cache entries, access logs and telemetry follow the serving Node's Region ... Every `ai.semantic-cache` embedding provider MUST be in the serving Node's Region, and a Route whose candidates split on residency MUST guard `ai.semantic-cache` with `Policy.spec.when`, one Policy per residency class with distinct `slot` values". 08-security-and-identity.md Compliance: "Each `ai.semantic-cache` embedding provider MUST be in the Region of the residency class its `when` selects, and a request whose class differs from the Node's Region MUST NOT use the Semantic Cache: it is served uncached or fails closed with an `RZ-AI` code."
blocking.fix: Adopt the Security and identity rule word for word. Each embedding provider is in the Region of the residency class its `when` selects. A request whose residency class differs from the serving Node's Region MUST NOT use the Semantic Cache for lookup or store: it is served uncached, or fails closed with an `RZ-AI` code. Until OQ-ai-llm-gateway-9 supplies the Node Region input that Security and identity names, fail safe: a Route whose candidates split on residency MUST NOT attach `ai.semantic-cache`, and `ruralz bundle audit` reports any that do. Record in OQ-ai-llm-gateway-9 that Security and identity chose option (a).

blocking.section: Unified API / Surface decoder (Strict JSON); Native passthrough (edits table)
blocking.issue: The strict JSON rule compares member names only for exact repetition after unescaping. It does not cover names that differ only in case. The Go `encoding/json` v1 API, which Go 1.27 keeps on top of the v2 implementation, matches struct fields case-insensitively. Provider servers match exactly. Native passthrough reads fields with a decoder but edits bytes in place and forwards 'unknown fields' unchanged, so the decoder and the provider can see different cap and model members. Attack on an `openai` native Route: send {"max_completion_tokens":100000, "MAX_COMPLETION_TOKENS":16, ...}. A case-insensitive decoder takes C = 16 and reserves E + 16, and the editor writes C into the member it recognized. The provider ignores the upper-case member and applies 100000. Hidden reasoning is never streamed, and this document says 'only the provider's cap bounds it', so the model bills about 100k reasoning tokens before the streaming guard sees 16 visible tokens. Authoritative usage then settles far above the reservation, and repeating the request concurrently drains provider spend beyond any Token Budget. The same mismatch applies to `model`, `n` and `candidateCount`, and to `stream`.
blocking.evidence: Surface decoder: "Every `request.body` decode that CEL, a Policy or the decoder reads MUST reject invalid UTF-8 and repeated member names at any depth, compared after unescaping, so no reader sees a different `model`, cap, `stream` or MCP `method`." Native passthrough: "Everything else, including unknown fields, key order and cache markers, passes unchanged"; edit "Write C into the cap field; remove other cap fields". Streaming guard: "Hidden reasoning is never streamed, so only the provider's cap bounds it."
blocking.fix: Add to Strict JSON: member names match case-sensitively, byte for byte after unescaping, as `encoding/json/v2` does by default and as `jsontext` tokens allow. Case-insensitive v1 matching MUST NOT be used. Reject with `RZ-AI-002` any object with a member whose name equals a field the decoder or editor recognizes (`model`, every cap field in the Native APIs table, `stream`, `n`, `candidateCount`, `stream_options`, `method`, `params`, `name`) under Unicode case folding but not exactly. Add fixtures for case variants of each cap field on each native API.

blocking.section: Kafka, NATS JetStream and MQTT (Topic ingress: Retries and Poison message rows)
blocking.issue: The Node's own admission refusals halt consumption, and the retry rule contradicts itself. The Route's ratelimit 'admits per message' and rejects with 429, and the Retries row both retries 429 and never retries 'Policy denials'. Read as a Policy denial, the rejection is a deterministic failure that pauses the partition at once. Read as a retryable 429, it uses up the 5 attempts (target) and then pauses. Either way, a backlog larger than the Route's rate, the normal state after any downtime, pauses partitions until an operator steps in, so the Rate Limit acts as a kill switch rather than flow control. RZ-RT-005 is not classified at all. On JetStream, a message held by a paused Node is redelivered after AckWait to the next Node, which pauses in turn, so one refusal or poison message stalls the shared consumer on every Node. The document does not say so.
blocking.evidence: Line 446: "`authz.*`, `validation.json-schema` and `transform.request` read headers and value, and `ratelimit` admits per message." Line 453: "| Retries | Timeouts, 408, 429, 5xx and `RZ-RT-004` retry with capped backoff, at most 5 attempts (target); Policy denials, validation failures and other 4xx never retry |". Line 454: "| Poison message | A value over `maxRequestBodyBytes`, a deterministic failure or a last failed attempt pauses the partition or consumer and raises `ruralz_ingress_paused` ...".
blocking.fix: Split the outcomes into three classes. (1) Node backpressure: ratelimit rejections, RZ-RT-004 and RZ-RT-005 hold the message and pause fetching until the bucket refills or a capped backoff ends. They release the in-flight unit while waiting, never count as an attempt and never raise ruralz_ingress_paused; on JetStream, in-progress acknowledgments or the AckWait rule must cover the wait. (2) Deterministic failures (authz denials, validation failures, Upstream 4xx other than 408 and 429) pause at once. (3) Retryable Upstream outcomes (timeouts, Upstream 408, 429 and 5xx, RZ-UP leg failures) use the 5-attempt budget (target). State that a JetStream pause stalls the durable consumer on every Node and a Kafka pause only its partition, and add the MaxDeliver or Term choice to OQ-multi-protocol-10.

blocking.section: Kafka, NATS JetStream and MQTT (Topic ingress: Concurrency, Node backpressure and JetStream rows)
blocking.issue: The JetStream AckWait rule cannot be met as written, and it ignores pre-buffered messages. First, backpressure holds have no upper bound. Each capped backoff step is bounded, but a Rate Limit window or sustained RZ-RT-005 can repeat them without limit, and the doc says these holds never pause and never count as an attempt. Yet AckWait MUST exceed 'backpressure waits'. Second, the research the doc cites describes Consume() as a callback with pre-buffering, and messages start their AckWait when delivered into that buffer, not when the one-at-a-time processor reaches them. With a slow Upstream, buffered messages pass AckWait and are redelivered to other Nodes while still queued on the first. Both Nodes then process them. The added load slows processing further, so still more messages expire: a redelivery storm that feeds itself. If a MaxDeliver is ever set (listed as an option in OQ-multi-protocol-10), a message that keeps timing out is dropped by the server, which contradicts 'nothing commits silently'. The previous L1-4 fix required in-progress acknowledgments or the AckWait rule to cover the wait; the document leaves in-progress acknowledgments 'unresearched', and the AckWait rule cannot cover an unbounded wait.
blocking.evidence: Line 449: "| Concurrency | One message in flight per Kafka partition, or per JetStream consumer on each Node (target), one in-flight unit each |". Line 451: "| Node backpressure | A `ratelimit` denial (429 `RZ-RL`), `RZ-RT-004` or `RZ-RT-005` holds the message, releases its in-flight unit and delays the next fetch with capped backoff, never counting as an attempt or pausing |". Line 455: "| JetStream | `AckWait` MUST exceed attempts times the Route `timeout` plus backoff and backpressure waits, unless in-progress acknowledgments (unresearched) extend it |". Research (go-libraries-protocols.md): "`Consume()` (callback with pre-buffering)".
blocking.fix: In the JetStream row: (1) Set the Consume pre-buffer to the in-flight bound, one message per consumer per Node (target), so no message waits in a local buffer while its AckWait runs. Alternatively, count the pre-buffer's worst-case queue time in the AckWait formula. (2) Give JetStream backpressure a maximum hold H, for example 60 s (target). AckWait MUST exceed attempts x Route timeout + backoff + H. When H expires, the Node stops holding the message and lets AckWait redeliver it, which is not an attempt and not a pause. Count it in a metric. (3) Require MaxDeliver unlimited on ingress consumers until OQ-multi-protocol-10 decides between MaxDeliver and Term, so a redelivery never drops a message silently. (4) Add in-progress acknowledgments and the pre-buffer setting to the OQ-multi-protocol-10 spike, and add their nats.go source to the research file.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling)
blocking.issue: The throttle is still a denial-of-service path and still breaks the Bounded everything rule, for three reasons. (1) Delayed requests have no cap. An empty username bucket parks each request for up to 2 s, and no limit applies to how many requests wait. A flood against one username at 10,000 req/s holds about 20,000 requests (hypothesis) until the Node's in-flight or connection ceilings reject everyone. (2) The hash queue gives password hashing all GOMAXPROCS slots. The source key stays off until OQ-security-and-identity-6, and a flood of random usernames gets a fresh bucket for every attempt. Each attempt then runs a PBKDF2 hash (Control plane and GitOps uses 600,000 iterations (target) for its own accounts), so a few dozen requests per second per Node (hypothesis) keep every core hashing and starve all other Routes. (3) Random usernames also churn the 100,000-entry LRU and evict the victim's bucket. An evicted bucket comes back full at burst 10, which resets the throttle against the targeted user. The document also says the design 'never locks out', then concedes that under a flood the owner shares a 1-per-second rate with the attacker. In practice that is a lockout.
blocking.evidence: Line 400: "| Username bucket | Burst 10, refill 1 per second, in a 64-shard LRU of 100,000 usernames (target); an empty bucket delays up to 2 s (target), then RZ-AUTH-007, and never locks out |"; line 402: "| Hash queue | `GOMAXPROCS` slots, 4 × `GOMAXPROCS` waiters, 1 s deadline (target); overflow gets RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed |"; line 401: "off until OQ-security-and-identity-6, since a load balancer makes one shared key"; line 404: "under a flood against one username, its owner shares the bucket's rate"; System overview Design principles: "Bounded everything | Every queue, buffer, pool, retry, fan-out, retired snapshot and per-key bucket table (LRU) has a ceiling."
blocking.fix: (1) Cap delayed requests per Node, for example at 1,024 (target), and return RZ-AUTH-007 with Retry-After at once beyond that cap. Alternatively, drop the delay and reject at once. (2) Limit hash slots to a fraction of the CPU, for example max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) (target), and state the resulting verifications per core (hypothesis) at the OQ-security-and-identity-2 iteration count. (3) Create or refresh a username bucket only after the hash queue admits the attempt, and add a Node-wide rate for new usernames (for example 100 per second (target)) so that churn cannot evict live buckets at will. (4) Say that the success cache is sharded like the username LRU. (5) Replace 'never locks out' with 'no fixed lockout; a flood shares the username's rate, and a recent success-cache entry exempts its owner'.

blocking.section: Revocation
blocking.issue: Revocation entries do not have a bounded lifetime as written, so the 100,000-entry cap can fill with entries that never expire. (1) A subject cut-off expires 'after the issuer's stated maximum token lifetime', but no such field or setting exists. The Configuration model fixes the `auth.jwt` issuers[] fields to issuer, jwksUrl and audiences, and OQ-security-and-identity-1 option (a) does not list a maximum lifetime. (2) A jti entry 'expires with exp', but Ruralz Control never sees the token, and nothing requires the REST API entry to carry exp. The document also never says that `auth.jwt` rejects a token without exp, and such a token makes its entry permanent. (3) 'covering tokens without iat' does not say whether such tokens of the subject are refused or accepted.
blocking.evidence: Line 422: "**Expiry.** A `jti` entry expires with `exp`; a subject cut-off after the issuer's stated maximum token lifetime, covering tokens without `iat`."; line 423: "**Cap.** 100,000 entries per Cluster (target), alerting at 80% (target); tombstoning relieves it, and at the cap new entries are refused and audited."; Configuration model line 424: "| `auth.jwt` | `issuers[]` with `issuer`, `jwksUrl`, `audiences` |"; line 528: "(a) Algorithms, clock skew, required claims, duplicate-binding error".
blocking.fix: Add a per-issuer maximum token lifetime and a 'require exp' rule to OQ-security-and-identity-1 option (a). Until that question closes, state a fixed default, for example 24 h (target), and say that `auth.jwt` rejects a token without exp (RZ-AUTH-003). Require the revocation REST API entry to carry exp for a jti, capped at the maximum lifetime, so Ruralz Control can expire it without seeing the token. Say that a subject cut-off refuses every token of that subject that lacks iat until the cut-off lapses. Tombstoning relieves only API-key entries, so also say how an operator relieves a cap filled by jti entries, for example by replacing them with one subject cut-off.

non_blocking.suggestion: The 421 fallback only helps clients that retry, and most HTTP/1.1 clients do not. A keep-alive connection that was busy during the Hot Reload is not idle, so it stays open, and its next request to the auth.mtls Route fails. Send Connection: close on the next response of every connection still in the old mode. Also consider scoping the certificate request by SNI through GetConfigForClient, so browsers on non-mTLS hostnames do not show certificate prompts.

Each entry is signed separately, so a Node that reconnects or cold-starts near the 100,000-entry cap (target) verifies up to 100,000 signatures, several seconds of one core (hypothesis). Have the signed high-water mark cover a digest or Merkle root of the entry set, so a snapshot needs one verification.

Marks are re-signed every 10 s and count as stale only after 30 s, so a relay can withhold an entry for up to 30 s (target) before a Node notices. Say that the detection bound for withholding is 30 s. Also state the clock-skew assumption behind mark age.

The unknown-kid refresh is limited per Node, but anonymous clients can trigger it on every Node. At 10,000 Nodes (target), random kid values drive about 333 JWKS fetches per second (hypothesis) to one IdP. blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling); Threat model (T1)
blocking.issue: The document claims a property the design does not have. T1 and the throttle table say the throttle 'never locks out'. But the username bucket (burst 10, refill 1 per second) is shared by the attacker and the real owner. A flood of wrong passwords for one username keeps that bucket empty, so the owner's verifications that miss the success cache wait 2 s and get 429 RZ-AUTH-007 for as long as the flood lasts. That is a targeted lockout, and the residual-trade-off sentence effectively admits it. The document also leaves two things undefined that an operator needs to judge the risk. It does not say whether a success-cache hit refreshes the 60 s entry, which decides whether a steady legitimate client is ever re-throttled. It does not say whether an unknown username computes a hash. Without that rule, an attacker who sprays many usernames gets a fresh burst of 10 for each and can fill the Node-wide hash queue (GOMAXPROCS slots, 4 x GOMAXPROCS waiters). Every `auth.basic` caller outside the success cache then gets 429.
blocking.evidence: Line 86: "| T1 | Credential guessing, hash-cost exhaustion, targeted lockout | TB-1 | 128-bit keys; [throttle](#pre-authentication-throttling) that delays, never locks out |". Line 400: "| Username bucket | Burst 10, refill 1 per second, in a 64-shard LRU of 100,000 usernames (target); an empty bucket delays up to 2 s (target), then RZ-AUTH-007, and never locks out |". Line 402: "| Hash queue | `GOMAXPROCS` slots, 4 x `GOMAXPROCS` waiters, 1 s deadline (target); overflow gets RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed |". Line 404: "Residual trade-off (T1, OQ-security-and-identity-15): under a flood against one username, its owner shares the bucket's rate."
blocking.fix: (1) Replace 'never locks out' with an accurate statement, for example "no permanent lockout; under a sustained flood against one username, that user is throttled while the flood lasts (residual, OQ-security-and-identity-15)". Or change the design so the owner is protected, for example by giving a separate small bucket to sources that authenticated that username successfully in the last 24 h (target). (2) State that a success-cache hit refreshes the entry, or that it does not. (3) State how unknown usernames are handled, for example "an unknown username computes one dummy hash under the same bucket and queue". Add a sentence and a T1 note that spraying across usernames is bounded only by the Node-wide hash queue, with the metric that exposes it. (4) Add both residuals to OQ-security-and-identity-15.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling); Threat model (T1)
blocking.issue: The basic-auth hash queue can use every core on a Node. An anonymous attacker can then pin all CPUs with PBKDF2 and slow every Route on the Node, not only auth.basic Routes. Per-username buckets do not stop this, because each new username gets a fresh burst of 10 and the LRU holds 100,000 usernames. The source key stays off until OQ-security-and-identity-6. The document never says whether an unknown username computes a hash: if it does not, the fast 401 lets an attacker enumerate usernames by timing; if it does, unknown usernames are the cheapest way to burn CPU. Nothing bounds the PBKDF2 iteration count either.
blocking.evidence: Line 402: "| Hash queue | `GOMAXPROCS` slots, 4 × `GOMAXPROCS` waiters, 1 s deadline (target); overflow gets RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed |". Line 400: "Burst 10, refill 1 per second, in a 64-shard LRU of 100,000 usernames (target)". Line 401: "off until OQ-security-and-identity-6". Line 529: OQ-2 option (a) "PBKDF2 with iteration count" gives no bound.
blocking.fix: Cap hashing at a share of the Node: max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) slots plus a Node-wide hash rate, both (target). Put every username that no credential declares into one shared bucket. Make unknown usernames compute a dummy hash under the same queue. Bound the iteration count in the OQ-security-and-identity-2 schema. Add Node-wide CPU exhaustion to T1.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling); Threat model (T1)
blocking.issue: T1 claims a property the design does not have, and the delay is unbounded. (1) One wrong attempt per second keeps a victim's bucket empty, so each of the victim's own requests that misses the success cache waits 2 s and gets 429: a targeted lockout while the flood lasts, which T1 says is mitigated. (2) No limit is stated on concurrent delayed requests. Each held request keeps a goroutine, a connection and its buffered request for up to 2 s, about 200,000 parked requests at 100,000 attempts per second (hypothesis). (3) Buckets are per Node, so N Nodes allow N guesses per second against one account, and no fleet-wide rate is stated.
blocking.evidence: Line 86: "| T1 | Credential guessing, hash-cost exhaustion, targeted lockout | TB-1 | 128-bit keys; [throttle](#pre-authentication-throttling) that delays, never locks out |". Line 400: "an empty bucket delays up to 2 s (target), then RZ-AUTH-007, and never locks out". Line 404: "under a flood against one username, its owner shares the bucket's rate."
blocking.fix: Bound delayed requests per bucket (for example 2) and per Node (target), and answer overflow at once with 429 RZ-AUTH-007. Reword T1 and the row to 'no permanent lockout; while a flood lasts, the attacked username is throttled, and the success cache is the owner's escape'. State whether a cache hit refreshes its entry. State the fleet-wide rate as N × 1 guess per second per username (target) in OQ-security-and-identity-15.

blocking.section: Authentication (JWT and OIDC); Revocation; Threat model (T2, T3)
blocking.issue: A leaked IdP signing key cannot be evicted quickly. Keys live up to 24 hours, refresh at half-life, and a new Revision reuses the keys of unchanged issuers, so a withdrawn kid keeps being accepted for up to 12 hours, plus 1 hour if the attacker also blocks the JWKS fetch. No (issuer, kid) revocation entry and no forced refetch exist. 'Outlive failed refreshes by 1 hour' contradicts System overview TB-10 if it means one hour past max-age.
blocking.evidence: Line 165: "Keys live for `max-age` clamped to 5 minutes to 24 hours ... refresh at half-life, and outlive failed refreshes by 1 hour as a degraded state (target); then RZ-AUTH-006." Line 164: "reuse unchanged issuers' keys". System overview TB-10: "Cached keys until expiry, then fail closed".
blocking.fix: Add an (issuer, kid) revocation entry delivered within 5 s at p99 (target), and an operator-forced JWKS refetch through the revocation API and the file-mode revocation file. Lower the upper clamp, for example to 6 hours (target). Define the grace as ending no later than max-age, or record a TB-10 amendment in OQ-security-and-identity-29. Add IdP key eviction to T2 or T3.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling); Transport security (Mutual TLS); Revocation
blocking.issue: Two verification caches outlive the removal of a credential, and basic credentials and client certificates have no revocation path. The basic success cache (60 s) has no stated flush on snapshot swap or revocation advance and no stated non-sliding TTL, and its digest may be a fast unkeyed hash. mTLS results are cached per connection and Policy, so a stolen certificate on a long-lived HTTP/2 connection may survive removal of its CA. No CRL, OCSP or serial entry exists.
blocking.evidence: Line 399: "| Success cache | Verified credential digests for 60 s, at most 10,000 per Node (target); a hit skips throttle and hash |". Line 130: "caches the result per connection and Policy". The Revocation table (lines 410-418) has no auth.basic or auth.mtls row.
blocking.fix: Success cache: an absolute TTL counted from verification, flushed on every swap and revocation-sequence advance, keyed by HMAC under a per-process key. Key the mTLS cache by compiled snapshot. Add Revocation rows for basic credentials (urgent entry by username) and client certificates (issuer and serial, plus a CRL field under OQ-security-and-identity-3), each Planned (Mx) with a propagation time tagged (target).

blocking.section: Secrets (rules 5 and 6); Threat model (T18)
blocking.issue: The proposed rules that close T18 can be bypassed, and the residual risk is not stated. Rule 6 misses 0.0.0.0 and ::, IPv4-mapped and NAT64 metadata forms, fd00:ec2::254 (unique-local, not link-local), redirects including https to http, and proxy environment variables. Rule 5 leaves in-root secrets exposed (listener key, admin TLS directory, Vault credential): a Bundle author can name any in-root file as an AIProvider apiKey with an attacker baseUrl, or as an upstream-oauth2 clientSecret with an attacker tokenUrl, and the Node sends it out. Rule 7 only flags this for review.
blocking.evidence: Line 347: "refuses loopback, link-local and metadata addresses, checked on the resolved address at connect time, unless `RURALZ_FETCH_ALLOW` lists them". Line 346: "A Node refuses to start if the root contains `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}` or the admin or Enrollment token file." Line 103: "| T18 | Secret exfiltration, SSRF by a Bundle author | TB-3, TB-10 | [Secrets](#secrets) rules 5 to 7 |".
blocking.fix: Normalize mapped and NAT64 addresses, and list the refused ranges (0.0.0.0/8, ::/128, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, 169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10, fd00:ec2::254). Re-check every redirect hop, never follow https to http, never follow redirects for tokenUrl, and ignore proxy variables unless allowlisted. Extend the rule 5 start-up refusal to RURALZ_ADMIN_TLS_DIR and the Vault credential. Scope the kubernetes provider by resourceNames. State the residual risk in T18, and propose a secret-to-destination binding under OQ-security-and-identity-22.

blocking.section: Transport security; Threat model (T10); Open questions (OQ-security-and-identity-29)
blocking.issue: The document contradicts System overview TB-4 ('TLS and authentication'): it accepts State Store URLs without credentials as a degraded state, and OQ-29 relaxes only the TLS wording. State Store tampering is missing from the threat model. A host that can reach an unauthenticated Redis can poison Response Cache and Semantic Cache entries served to every client, and can reset GCRA, Quota and Token Budget state.

Line 95: "| T10 | State Store eavesdropping, cross-user cache hits | TB-4 | TLS when configured; principal in cache keys |". Line 555: OQ-29 only proposes "TLS when configured; cleartext reported". System overview TB-4: "TLS and authentication; contents are never configuration".

blocking.section: Control plane security (Admin ports); Threat model (T14)
blocking.issue: One admin token serves both metrics scrapers and /tap, /config/dump and /debug/*. A stolen scrape config therefore gives /tap (live bodies and PII), /config/dump (every key hash, which feeds T19) and /debug/*. Logging detects the misuse only afterward.
blocking.evidence: Line 476: "The token, scrapers included, is accepted only over TLS or loopback; without one, other paths return 401. `/tap` sessions and `/config/dump` reads are logged." Line 534: "(a) Two `RURALZ_ADMIN_*` settings".

Compare tokens in constant time. Update OQ-7 to three settings and the pack section 2 amendment. Extend T14 to scraper-token theft.

blocking.section: Compliance (Data residency); Threat model (T21)
blocking.issue: T21 claims Compliance mitigates residency violations in logs and telemetry, but Compliance constrains only the Semantic Cache. A residency-class request that reaches an out-of-Region Node is served there, and its logs, traces and gen_ai telemetry are written in that Region. No fail-closed rule, content stripping or residual risk is stated.
blocking.evidence: Line 106: "| T21 | Residency violation by generation, embedding, cache, logs or telemetry | TB-3, TB-4, TB-12 | [Compliance](#compliance) |". Line 520 constrains only the Semantic Cache. AI/LLM gateway line 597: "access logs and telemetry follow the serving Node's Region, to which operators steer clients".
blocking.fix: Add a per-class rule for requests whose class differs from the Node's Region: strict classes are rejected with an RZ-AI code, and other classes are served with content-free telemetry and no Semantic Cache. State the residual steering risk in T21 and fold the rule into the OQ-ai-llm-gateway-9 answer.

blocking.section: Revocation (Expiry); Authentication (JWT and OIDC); Open questions (OQ-security-and-identity-1)
blocking.issue: Subject revocation depends on an undefined field ('the issuer's stated maximum token lifetime'), which is neither in the Configuration model nor in any Open question. If the value is unknown, cut-offs either fill the cap or expire too soon, and revoked long-lived tokens are accepted again. exp is never stated as required, so a signed token without exp never expires and its jti entry has no expiry.
blocking.evidence: Line 422: "A `jti` entry expires with `exp`; a subject cut-off after the issuer's stated maximum token lifetime, covering tokens without `iat`." Configuration model line 424 fixes only "`issuers[]` with `issuer`, `jwksUrl`, `audiences`". Line 528: OQ-1 option (a) names no lifetime.
blocking.fix: Require exp and reject tokens without it (RZ-AUTH-003). Add a per-issuer maximum token lifetime to OQ-1 option (a) (proposed, default such as 24 hours (target)). Reject tokens whose exp is beyond that bound, and expire subject cut-offs after it. The body is 4,961 of 5,000 words, so make matching cuts.

non_blocking.suggestion: A detached restart forgets revocation entries, so crashing a Node during a Ruralz Control outage brings revoked credentials back. Recommend OQ-security-and-identity-5 option (b), or name the residual risk in T17.
Consider an opt-in fail-closed posture for high-assurance Routes when the mark age passes a bound (target).

Refuse any secret-bearing hop to a non-loopback address without TLS (AIProvider apiKey over an http baseUrl, a redis:// URL with a password, OAuth2 tokens toward http Upstreams), whatever OQ-29 decides.

Give an excludePolicies change that removes authentication diff impact security, offer a way to declare public Routes under a non-overridable Gateway auth Policy, and note that before M2 anonymous Routes are reported only by metrics.
RZ-AUTH-004 and RZ-AUTH-005 act as an oracle. Return RZ-AUTH-002 to clients and keep the detailed codes in telemetry.
Handle tokens without a kid, bind JWK kty and alg to the token alg, reject unknown crit headers, cap the JWKS size and key count (target), and follow no redirects on jwksUrl.
auth.jwt forwards bearer tokens to third-party Upstreams. Recommend stripping Authorization there and having ruralz bundle audit report it.
Re-normalize a path rewritten by transform.request after authz, and keep it within the matched prefix.

State the residual risk of cross-Consumer data carried in a pool's globals, consider per-Consumer pools, and align the credential Capability with OQ-wasm-plugin-system-3 (b), covering Set-Cookie and credentials in bodies.
Add negative caching with backoff for failed auth.upstream-oauth2 fetches.

blocking.section: Rate limiting / Decision path; Failure matrix
blocking.issue: The document claims the first-seen key budget caps State Store calls at B per Cell "whatever N", but the per-Node share is B / N_published. The document itself says N_published can be absent or lag N_serving. In file mode no clusterNodeCount exists, so the per-Node budget is undefined. Read as N = 1, every Node gets the full B, and the Cell makes N x B calls per second. During the scale-out lag the document describes elsewhere, the cost is N_serving / N_published x B. The stated bound and the headroom figure of "20% of a shard" are therefore false in two ordinary states.
blocking.evidence: Step 3: "spends one unit of a per-Node budget, max(1, B / N_published) per second across all Policies, with B = 20,000 per Cell, 20% of a shard (hypothesis)" and "First-seen keys thus cost at most B calls per second per Cell, whatever N and the Policy count". Per-Node ceiling: "else derived from N_published, the `HeartbeatReply` `clusterNodeCount`, else the full limit with a degraded metric" and "scaling 10 to 100 Nodes keeps N_serving / N_published up to 10 for about 34 minutes (hypothesis)". Scenario: a key-rotation flood during that scale-out makes 10 x 20,000 = 200,000 first-seen GCRA calls per second, about 2 shards' worth at the document's own 100,000 per shard (hypothesis). In file mode with 100 Nodes it is 2,000,000 per second.
blocking.fix: Define the per-Node budget when N_published is absent, for example a fixed 200 per second per Node (target), and state the resulting bound N x 200. Restate the bound as B x N_serving / N_published, noting that it grows during the count qualification window. Add both cases to the "Key-rotation flood or new Node" failure-matrix row and to OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-19 and -20.

blocking.section: Rate limiting / Decision path; Failure matrix
blocking.issue: The failure matrix labels the local-only path "Open", but for established legitimate keys it fails closed, and an attacker can force it across a Cell. A local-only entry has capacity 1 and refills at 2 x requests / N_published per window. That is below the per-Node ceiling of max(10, 2 x requests / N) that the document gives pinned clients, and capacity 1 allows no burst. Legitimate keys reach this path in two ways. First, every restarted Node, and so every Node during a rolling Zero-Downtime Upgrade, starts empty. Second, a key-rotation flood fills the shared 1,048,576-entry CLOCK table, which evicts established entries, and uses up the shared first-seen budget, so evicted keys come back as local-only for as long as the flood lasts.
blocking.evidence: "Past it, it gets a local-only entry for 10 s or until evicted (target): capacity 1, refill 2 × `requests` / N_published per window, no GCRA."; "A new Node, after scale-out or a Zero-Downtime Upgrade, starts empty: 50,000 active keys on 100 Nodes leave local-only in about 250 s (hypothesis)."; "Buckets, local-only and over-limit entries share a Node-wide budget of 1,048,576 entries"; matrix row "Key-rotation flood or new Node | `ratelimit` | First-seen keys past the Cell budget ... go local-only | Open". Scenario: a Consumer with limit 100 per 1s on 100 Nodes sends 50 rps over one pinned HTTP/2 connection. Normally the per-Node ceiling of 10 applies. While local-only, the Node admits 2 per second with no burst and returns 429 RZ-RL-001 for the rest. That lasts up to about 250 s after each upgrade, and for the whole of an IPv6 source-rotation flood (OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-18 is open).
blocking.fix: Give local-only entries the Policy's per-Node ceiling as capacity and refill, so admission stays within pack 8.8's N x per-Node ceiling bound. Keep one-hit keys from evicting entries that have already had a GCRA answer, for example with a second-sighting admission filter or a separate segment for local-only entries. Split the matrix row: new keys are Open, bounded by N x ceiling; established keys evicted or on a fresh Node give the stated under-admission (Closed), quantified and tagged (hypothesis).

blocking.section: Response caching; Failure matrix
blocking.issue: Every partition of a URI shares one hash tag, so one Redis Cluster slot. The Principal rule makes authenticated Routes key per principal by default. A popular authenticated URI therefore sends every principal's lookup script, including its SET NX lease, to one shard. The hot-entry layer does not help, because it only absorbs one entry read by many Nodes, not many distinct entries in one slot. When that shard saturates, its State client breaker opens on every Node, and every ratelimit, quota and ai.token-budget key hashed to that shard falls to failureMode. The Response Cache thus disables unrelated limits. The failure matrix bounds reads per entry, never per URI slot.
blocking.evidence: "Layout | One hash tag per URI, `{<SHA-256 of scheme, host, path, normalized query>}`, holds a metadata key (generation, `Vary` names), a fill lease and at most 8 variants per partition (target)"; "Principal | `auth.*` Routes key per principal unless `config.key` replaces it"; "A shard serves about 100,000 calls per second (hypothesis)"; matrix: "Hot, expiring or invalidated cache entry | ... At most N reads per second per entry (target)". Scenario: GET /v1/me behind auth.jwt with 150,000 active principals at 1 rps each gives about 150,000 lookup scripts per second on one slot (hypothesis), above one shard's capacity. The shard breaker opens, and the Rate Limits of every Consumer whose key hashes to that shard fail open.
blocking.fix: Choose and state one design. (a) Tag each variant by URI plus partition, and keep the per-URI generation in its own key, read in the same pipelined batch (pack 8.7 rule 3), so invalidation still bumps one key. (b) Cap lookups per URI slot per Node (target) and bypass the cache above the cap as a degraded state. Either way, add a failure-matrix row "Hot URI slot" giving the per-slot ceiling (hypothesis), the Open behavior, and the effect on limit keys that share the shard.

blocking.section: Load balancing
blocking.issue: Round-robin schedules have a floor of 65,536 slots per Upstream regardless of Endpoint count, because the size is the max of the two values, not the min. Rings reach 1 MiB each. No Node-wide bound covers them, and Data plane's worst-case Node memory sum does not include them. Copy-on-write rebuilds briefly hold two copies. LB structures therefore grow without bound with the Upstream count in a Bundle.

blocking.section: Circuit breakers; Timeouts, deadlines, retries and hedging; Failure matrix (Zone lost, black-holed)
blocking.issue: The zone-blackhole analysis covers only new dials. Attempts already on pooled connections, which is every attempt on an HTTP/2 or gRPC Upstream, hang until perTryTimeout. The document sets no HTTP/2 connection health check, and Go's transport has none by default. Under the proposed defaults perTryTimeout = 15 / (1 + 1) = 7.5 s, and timeout is not in the default retryOn. Failure scenario: a zone holding one third of an HTTP/2 Upstream's Endpoints goes dark at 1,000 attempts per second per Node. About 333 attempts per second each hold a maxConnections slot for 7.5 s, which would need about 2,500 slots. The 1,024 slots fill in about 3 s and the 256 pending slots fill at once. From then on all traffic to the Upstream, healthy-zone traffic included, gets 503 RZ-UP-006 on every Node at once, until ejection at about 7.5 s. Meanwhile one third of requests hang 7.5 s and end with 504 RZ-UP-003. The figure of 333 of 1,024 slots is false for pooled traffic.
blocking.evidence: "A dial holds its slot at most 1 s (target): at 1,000 attempts per second per Node, a black-holed third of Endpoints holds about 333 of 1,024 slots until ejected (hypothesis), fewer under `least-request`."; "| `retries.perTryTimeout` | Leg time left divided by (retries left + 1) (target) |"; "| Zone lost, black-holed | Load balancing | Dials fail at 1 s (target) as connect errors, retry and eject after `consecutiveErrors`; pooled requests end at `perTryTimeout`; the ratio guard holds the breaker | Open | ..."; research section 6: "x/net/http2 | `PingTimeout` defaults to 15 s; `ReadIdleTimeout` 0 = no health check".
blocking.fix: Add HTTP2Config pings after about 1 s of read idleness with a 1 s timeout (target), so a dead pooled connection fails as connect or reset and its streams retry elsewhere. Eject an Endpoint on its first attempt timeout while other attempts to it are in flight, or cap in-flight attempts per Endpoint at about 2 x its weighted share of maxConnections (target). Recompute the slot figure for pooled traffic, tagged (hypothesis). Split the failure-matrix row into dial and pooled cases, giving the time to ejection and the RZ-UP-006 exposure for each.

blocking.section: Response caching; Failure matrix (State Store out of memory)
blocking.issue: The Response Cache shares the noeviction State Store with limit keys, and nothing bounds the rate of stores between 10 s memory polls. Take 10,000 distinct cacheable misses per second at 128 KiB, about 1.3 GB/s: the 30% headroom of a 16 GiB shard fills in under 4 s. The store reaches OOM and Redis refuses every write script, so all Rate Limits fail open and every ai.token-budget returns 503 Cell-wide. With noeviction and TTLs of up to 25 h, skipping new stores does not free memory, so this can last for hours.
blocking.evidence: "The State Store holding limit keys MUST run `maxmemory-policy noeviction`."; "Nodes read `INFO memory` every 10 s off the request path and skip stores above 70% of `maxmemory` (target)."; "with TTL of freshness plus the larger stale window"; "at most 24 h, stale windows at most 1 h (target)"; "| State Store out of memory | Limit scripts; cache stores | Stores skipped above 70% (target); at OOM limits fail open | Open; Closed for `ai.token-budget` |".

blocking.section: Observability principles / Cardinality and overhead budgets (Overhead per signal)
blocking.issue: The new Ruralz-owned aggregates are sharded per P, but the memory figure is too small for contention-free sharding, and nothing bounds the shard count. Four 8-byte counter shards in 120 bytes share one 64-byte cache line, so every core still bounces the same line and sharding gains nothing over one atomic. Padding each shard to a cache line costs 4 x 64 = 256 bytes per counter series at 4 P, more than twice the budgeted 120. Memory also grows linearly with GOMAXPROCS, which the document never caps. At 32 P, padded shards cost about 2 KiB per counter series and about 6 KiB per histogram label set: roughly 100 MB for 50,000 counter series plus about 19 MB for 3,125 histogram label sets. That is several times the 24 MiB metrics budget and the 40 MiB all-telemetry budget. Separately, Go exposes no public API for the current P index. The usual route is a go:linkname to runtime.procPin, a runtime internal that Go keeps only for compatibility, and the tech stack has no row for it.
blocking.evidence: Observability principles: "Metric values live in Ruralz-owned aggregates, not SDK synchronous instruments: atomic counters and histogram buckets per label set, sharded per P and kept by name across Hot Reloads." Overhead per signal: "Metrics memory assumes 120 bytes per counter or gauge series, 700 per histogram label set over 4 P and 120 per series for one collection (hypothesis), pending an M1 heap benchmark." Table row: "| Metrics | 2 µs or less for 40 operations (hypothesis) | 0 (target) | 24 MiB or less at the series cap (hypothesis) |"
blocking.fix: Shard only the hot families that every request touches: the listener-scoped series (ruralz_http_listener_requests_total, ruralz_http_gateway_duration_seconds, ruralz_http_active_requests, body sizes) and fixed families. Pad each shard to a cache line and cap shards at min(GOMAXPROCS, 8) (target). Per-Route, per-Policy and per-Upstream label sets already spread contention across label sets, so they can use one unpadded atomic per value. State where the shard index comes from without runtime internals, for example a stripe chosen per connection or per pooled request context. Restate the memory model as a function of shard count, recompute the Metrics and All-telemetry rows at the reference GOMAXPROCS and at 32, and make the M1 heap and contention benchmark run at both.

blocking.section: Cardinality and overhead budgets (Cardinality budget)
blocking.issue: The Hot Reload churn bound contradicts Data plane, and the memory budget does not cover churn. Data plane keeps K = 2 retired snapshots plus at most one closing snapshot, and the closing one stays pinned for a 30 s grace period. Up to four snapshots, each possibly with a disjoint Route name set, can therefore reference label sets at once. The document says release happens after 'active plus K = 2 retired' and bounds churn at 3 times. Either label sets of the closing snapshot are released while its requests still record into them, or the real bound is 4 times. In either case the retained label sets multiply memory: 3 or 4 times the per-Revision worst case can exceed the '24 MiB or less at the series cap' and '40 MiB or less' rows. Long-lived WebSocket or SSE sessions keep retired snapshots pinned for hours, so this multiple can persist and is not transient.
blocking.evidence: Cardinality budget: "a dropped name is exported until the last snapshot referencing it retires (active plus K = 2 retired, per [Data plane](03-data-plane.md#configuration-snapshots-and-hot-reload)), then released" and "A CI test of 1,000 Hot Reloads, each renaming every Route, MUST stay within 3 times the single-Revision worst case (hypothesis)". Data plane: "| Retired snapshots | K = 2 (target), plus at most one closing |" and "After a grace period of 30 s (target), anything still pinned ends with RZ-RT-014".
blocking.fix: Count the closing snapshot. Either state the bound as 4 times (active, two retired, one closing) and change the CI test to match, or release a snapshot's label sets when it becomes closing and route its late records to _overflow. Then either budget metrics memory at that churn multiple, adjusting the Metrics and All-telemetry rows and OQ-observability-17, or add a Node-wide ceiling on retiring label sets. Beyond that ceiling, the oldest retiring sets fold into _overflow. Keep per-Revision admission independent of retiring sets so that folding stays identical on every Node.

blocking.issue: The SLO-AI-1 SLI is mathematically wrong under the AI/LLM gateway's own settlement table. That table records an attempt with reported usage in ruralz_ai_settlements_total and an attempt without usage in ruralz_ai_usage_missing_total, so the two outcomes are disjoint. 1 - missing / settlements is then not a good-over-total ratio. With 100 settled and 100 missing it reads 0% instead of 50%, and with more missing than settled it goes negative. That breaks the objective and any burn-rate rule built on it. The catalog row ('SLO-AI-1 denominator') does not say whether charge-all-of-R settlements count, so two implementers would build different SLIs.

AI/LLM gateway: "| Usage reported | Any attempt | That usage, summed over attempts; rest of R released | ruralz_ai_settlements_total |" and "| Attempt reached the provider, no usage read | ... | All of R for that attempt | ruralz_ai_usage_missing_total by reason |".
blocking.fix: Define the SLI as 1 − missing / (settlements + missing), both summed over provider and model. blocking.section: CI stages
blocking.issue: The document says binaries can ship from stage 4, a pr-fast job. The Release document says one tagged workflow builds, signs and publishes every artifact. blocking.section: Unit and property tests
blocking.issue: The document requires every unit test to run under the race detector, and it builds with CGO_ENABLED=0 (G1, ADR-0001). It never says how these two fit together. On linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and windows/amd64, `go test -race` needs cgo and a C toolchain, and it stops with '-race requires cgo' when CGO_ENABLED=0. Turning cgo on for the race jobs fixes that, but then the tests run with the cgo DNS resolver and cgo `os/user`, not the pure-Go code that ships. So no pull-request stage runs the tests in the configuration that is actually released. Repository layout already allows this ('The race detector MAY enable cgo for test binaries'), but this document owns the pipelines and does not say so.
blocking.evidence: Unit and property tests: "Unit tests are hermetic: time, randomness and the State Store arrive as failure-injecting fakes, and tests run shuffled under the race detector." Test pyramid: "`pr-fast` builds the three binaries with `CGO_ENABLED=0` for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (... gate G1 ...); shipped binaries come only from `release`."
blocking.fix: Add one sentence: 'Race jobs set CGO_ENABLED=1 for test binaries only, with the `netgo,osusergo` build tags; a second `pr-fast` job runs the same tests without -race under CGO_ENABLED=0, so the shipped configuration is tested.' To keep the length band, shorten the next sentence.

blocking.section: Benchmarks and regression gates
blocking.issue: The alloc/op gate has no baseline that any stage produces. The regression policy compares against 'the latest `main` result on the same hardware'. But the `main` stage runs only end-to-end and secret-leak tests (Figure 1), microbenchmarks run only in `pr-full` and `nightly`, and `pr-full` runs on shared general runners, where 'same hardware' cannot be guaranteed from one job to the next. A pull request's merge base can also be behind the latest `main`, so an unrelated regression that has already merged would be blamed on the pull request.
blocking.evidence: Regression policy: "against the default-branch baseline, the latest `main` result on the same hardware." Figure 1: "main: end-to-end on Docker Compose and kind, secret leak tests". Test pyramid: "| Benchmarks | ... | `pr-full`; `nightly` |". nightly jobs table: only the latency job runs on "Reference hardware, alone".
blocking.fix: Define the baseline for each gate. alloc/op: the same `pr-full` job benchmarks the merge base and the head on the same runner, interleaved, with at least 10 runs each (target). Macro latency: the previous `nightly` latency result on the reference hardware. Release: the release job re-runs the previous release's benchmarks on the same machine.

blocking.section: Plugin SDK and AI provider harnesses (AI provider mock)
blocking.issue: The 'Mid-stream error' case puts the commit point at the first chunk. The AI/LLM gateway puts it at the first content event, and it requires Provider Fallback for a stream error before content. An Anthropic stream always opens with `message_start`, which carries no content. So an `error` event after `message_start` but before any content block must fall back to the next candidate. This harness would assert the opposite and fail a correct implementation, or push implementers into the wrong behavior.
blocking.evidence: AI provider mock: "**Mid-stream error.** After the first chunk, the Node MUST NOT attempt Provider Fallback; it ends the stream with an `RZ-AI` error event." AI/LLM gateway, fallback matrix: "| Timeout or stream error before content | `perTryTimeout`, Anthropic `error`, Bedrock `modelStreamErrorException` | No | Yes | If exhausted |" and Figure 2: "AP-->>GW: status 200 and first content event / GW-->>C: response headers, now committed". Glossary: Provider Fallback "only before the response is committed".
blocking.fix: Replace the bullet with: '**Mid-stream error.** An error before the first content event (Anthropic `error` after `message_start`, Bedrock `modelStreamErrorException`) MUST cause Provider Fallback; after it, the Node ends the stream with `RZ-AI-009` and never falls back.'

non_blocking.suggestion: Fixing `GOGC` and `GOMAXPROCS` does not stop GC cycles from clearing `sync.Pool`, so 'cannot flake' overstates it. Use `GOGC=off` for the alloc gate, or integer `testing.AllocsPerRun` counts. Also note that at the seed of 30 allocations or fewer (hypothesis), a single added allocation (about 3.3%) already breaks the 3% (target) threshold. The performance document should confirm that this is intended.

SM-9 is a p95 figure, but the row does not say how many Rollouts the nightly scale job runs to compute it, or that Plugins are cached, which SM-9 requires. State the repetition count, for example 20 or more Rollouts per run (target).

The AI stream parser oracle 'Extracted usage equals the fixture's final usage' only holds if the fuzzer changes where the fixture is split into chunks, not what the chunks contain. State that, and for mutated content use the oracle 'no panic; either the correct usage or usage reported missing'.

Traffic management says a `NOSCRIPT` fallback is resent as `EVAL` 'within the same deadline'. Assert that in the `EVALSHA` scenario, so the retry never extends the Policy's single bounded State Store call.

Redis Cluster and Valkey cluster built from generic containers announce container IPs that the host test process cannot reach on Docker Desktop. Either run the test process on the container network or state that this scenario runs only on Linux CI runners.

Several Ruralz Control replicas and Nodes in one process need separate `RURALZ_DATA_DIR` locks, and they must not share global OpenTelemetry or `slog` state. Say that each component instance gets its own providers and data directory.

The AI/LLM gateway settles per attempt: R is charged for each attempt that returned no usage, and usage is summed across attempts. Phrase the Token Budget property per attempt. Also carry over the gateway's caveat about hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama` (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17).

'runs outside Ruralz CI' contradicts the `pr-full` CI stage in the same table. Write 'also runs outside Ruralz CI'. Also say which suite 'The suite also re-runs the JSON-Schema-Test-Suite' refers to (the configuration suite).

Add `/tap` output to the list of places the canary secret must not appear, and exclude `/debug/pprof` heap profiles, which necessarily hold resolved secrets. In scenario 7, define a 'failed request' as an error seen by a client that honors `Connection: close` and GOAWAY.
The Control-mode Compose topology includes the AI provider mock, which is Planned (M3), but the topology is tagged Planned (M2). Tag the mock separately.

kind, Helm and the Autobahn test suite tool are named but have no tech stack catalog row or license research. Pack section 14 does not waive research for CI-only tooling. Add an Open question, owned by tech-stack-and-libraries, to catalog these test tools.

Repository layout stage 5 lists CLI tests on darwin/arm64 and windows/amd64 only. This document correctly adds darwin/amd64, as the tech stack requires. Flag this to the cross-document critic so Repository layout is updated.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: The rollback path after finalize contradicts the restore semantics in Control plane and GitOps and understates the outage. Restore runs into an empty deployment and opens a higher storeEpoch with a new online key. Without the operator's revocation list, every Node certificate issued before the restore is refused until re-enrollment, so every Node serves detached, not only the Nodes enrolled since the backup.
blocking.evidence: Ruralz Control upgrades, step 4: "After it, rollback means `ruralz control restore` from the first backup, losing every later Control Store write (Rollouts, audit entries, Enrollments); Nodes enrolled since re-enroll." Control plane and GitOps: "`ruralz control restore` runs only from the host CLI into an empty deployment ... without one, no Node certificate issued before the restore is admitted ... until its Node re-enrolls or the list arrives. Those Nodes serve detached."
blocking.fix: Rewrite step 4 to match Control plane and GitOps: restore with N-1 binaries into an empty deployment, a higher storeEpoch, a rotated online key, invalidated sessions and tokens, and the revocation list required, otherwise fleet-wide detached Nodes and re-enrollment. Link to Backup, restore and postgres, and give this cost as the reason for the soak.

blocking.evidence: "| Node upgrade handover | `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}` file lock, candidate, persisted `assignmentIndex`, Unix-socket readiness message |" versus Control plane and GitOps: "Nodes persist the highest pair activated under `${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}/identity/`".
blocking.fix: Replace assignmentIndex with the persisted (storeEpoch, assignmentSeq) pair, promotionSeq and the anchor-set version. Add identity/ to the surface and Control plane and GitOps as an owner, and keep format changes additive or version-marked.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: Neither State Store migration path preserves consumptive state. The two-step switch starts new Quota and Token Budget keys empty, which gives up to 2x admission for the whole window, not just for the propagation time. The hash-tag path splits counters while the Cluster runs mixed N and N-1, which is allowed indefinitely, unless the N script writes both keys. Both paths break P8 and pack 8.9.
blocking.evidence: "either keeps the replaced key's hash tag, so one script covers both keys, or switches in two steps ... may admit up to 2x a global limit for the signal's propagation time (hypothesis)"; "| Nodes within one Cluster | Any mix of N and N-1, at any time |".
blocking.fix: Allow only the shared-hash-tag path for consumptive state. The N script reads and writes both keys in one EVAL while N-1 Nodes can serve, then migrates lazily (read old, write new, delete old). Allow the two-step switch only for caches or at window boundaries, state bounds per state class (hypothesis), and hand them to Scalability and distributed state.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: The MUST that every release can roll back to every supported line fails once Bundles use N-only fields. A restart-based rollback (a Kubernetes image rollback or systemd) boots Last-Known-Good, gets RZ-CFG-024, NACKs the assigned Revision and stays not ready. That contradicts the rollback MUST and the claim that skew never costs an active Revision.
blocking.evidence: "A release MUST hand over from, and roll back to, every line in support"; "| Last-Known-Good and Node | ... | Newer field, booted by N-1 | RZ-CFG-024; the Node waits for the Control Stream or stays not ready (pack 8.2) |"; Figure 2 node k: "Oldest Node schema level rises; Bundles may use new fields".
blocking.fix: Qualify the MUST so that rollback holds only while the active Revision and Last-Known-Good use no field above N-1's levels. Mark Figure 2 node k as the point of no binary rollback without first rolling out a Revision without N-only fields. Have Ruralz Control flag such Clusters, recommend a soak before adopting new fields, and name Zero-downtime upgrades as the owner of the procedure.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: Before finalize, rule 2 keeps only replicated traffic readable by N-1. Local bbolt records, local snapshots, content objects and audit segments may be written in N formats, which breaks the 'normal rolling step' back to N-1. After finalize, nothing makes an N-1 binary halt on the version-advance entry or on N-only entries, so its FSM can silently diverge, and the skew table's Enforcement cell states no enforcement.
blocking.evidence: Step 2: "every replica writes only N-1 encodings in log entries, snapshots sent to followers and the write-forwarding and status-forwarding classes on 8092"; step 4: "Before finalize, returning any replica to N-1 is a normal rolling step."; "| Ruralz Control replicas | ... | N-2; an N-1 binary after finalize | [Ruralz Control upgrades](#ruralz-control-upgrades) |".
blocking.fix: Widen rule 2 to all persisted replica state. Add that a replica meeting a cluster version above its binary's, or an unknown entry type, stops before serving and exports a metric, never skipping the entry, and that the same check runs at startup against the snapshot and the log.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: The rule that N decodes only N-1 encodings is infeasible for two reasons. hashicorp/raft snapshots only after a threshold of new entries and keeps trailing logs, so low-write clusters keep N-2 or older encodings in the latest snapshot and in the logs sent to lagging or joining followers. Digest-addressed Revision content, diffs, plans and sealed audit segments are immutable and cannot be re-encoded.
blocking.evidence: "Ruralz Control upgrades one minor at a time, since N decodes only N-1 encodings"; "N binaries MUST decode every N-1 log entry, record and snapshot."; Control plane and GitOps: "| Revision content, diffs, plans, sealed audit segments | Content store, on a quorum before the referencing entry | Yes |".
blocking.fix: For Raft state: after the version advance commits, every replica takes a user snapshot past that index, truncates its trailing logs and reports to the leader, and the next upgrade is refused until every voter has reported. For immutable content: each object carries a format marker, and every release decodes every format still inside retention. Add this to Versioned surfaces.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: Rendering has no cluster-version gate. During a mixed-replica upgrade, N and N-1 leaders materialize different v1alpha1 defaults, so one commit yields leader-dependent digests. CI renders stop matching, and a promotion can carry into prod a default that staging never ran, before finalize.
blocking.evidence: "... whichever replica leads, so an election mid-upgrade is harmless."; "| `ruralz bundle push` to Ruralz Control | CLI at N; N-1 only if N's release notes list no `ruralz/v1alpha1` default change |"; pack 8.1: "Promotion | Moves a source commit, not a digest".
blocking.fix: Until finalize, all replicas render at the cluster version's schema levels and defaults. This is feasible because each v1alpha1 default change is a new schema level. The version advance never re-renders recorded Revisions, and the Configuration model owns level-pinned rendering.

blocking.section: Release cadence and support windows
blocking.issue: The claim of one maintenance window every 6 months conflicts with the procedure. Each Ruralz Control step needs a 24-hour soak and a finalize before the Nodes upgrade, and the next step needs every Node upgraded, so two minors take at least two sequential soaks and more than 48 hours.
blocking.evidence: "An operator can plan one maintenance window every 6 months (target) and stay supported; it contains two single-minor steps, each upgrading Ruralz Control and then the Nodes." versus "Once every voter reports N and a 24-hour soak (target) has passed, an operator finalizes" and Figure 2 "i --> h", "h --> m", "m --> j".
blocking.fix: State that the upgrade spans at least two soaks, about 2 to 3 days (target). Alternatively, let Node upgrades run in parallel with the soak once every voter reports N, and redraw Figure 2 with j after g.

blocking.section: Control Stream versioning
blocking.issue: Removing a field with `reserved` is allowed within v1 with no skew condition. If Ruralz Control N stops sending a field that an N-1 Node reads, the Node silently treats it as unset while buf breaking passes. Only additions are constrained.

blocking.fix: Allow removal only after at least 2 minor releases (target) during which no in-policy version reads or requires the field, with the sender still populating it meanwhile. Apply the rule in both directions, and run buf breaking against the last tag of every line inside the skew window.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew (Ruralz Control upgrades)
blocking.issue: Step 4 describes rollback after finalize as `ruralz control restore`, with only one Node consequence: Nodes enrolled since the backup re-enroll. That understates what restore does according to Control plane and GitOps, which owns `ruralz control restore`. Restore runs only into an empty deployment. It needs a root-signed anchor set with a new online key, which opens a higher `storeEpoch`. It invalidates all sessions and API tokens. Unless the operator supplies a revocation list, it admits no Node certificate issued before the restore, so every Node, not just recently enrolled ones, serves detached until it re-enrolls. Operators who follow this document would plan a rollback that behaves differently from what the owning document specifies.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew (Ruralz Control upgrades, Upgrade order, Figure 2)
blocking.issue: The Raft rules freeze wire and storage encodings at N-1 until finalize. They do not freeze rendering semantics. While binaries are mixed, Ruralz Control keeps building Revisions from Git. If minor N changes a `ruralz/v1alpha1` default, which line 75 allows, one commit renders to different digests depending on whether an N or an N-1 replica leads. An election mid-upgrade can therefore produce a different Revision, spurious Drift or an unplanned Rollout, and the new default reaches N-1 Nodes before the operator finalizes. Figure 2 also resumes pushes from an N CLI before finalize ('i' comes before 'h'). The N CLI computes the expected digest with N defaults. If N binaries rendered with N-1 defaults until finalize, which is what the encoding rule implies, that push fails with RZ-CFG-027.
blocking.evidence: Line 163: "While the cluster version is N-1, every replica writes only N-1 encodings in log entries, snapshots sent to followers and the write-forwarding and status-forwarding classes on 8092, whichever replica leads, so an election mid-upgrade is harmless." Line 148: "N-1 only if N's release notes list no `ruralz/v1alpha1` default change".

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew (Ruralz Control upgrades, Upgrade order)

After a finalize from N-2 to N-1, the latest Raft snapshot and the retained log entries can still hold N-2 encodings until a new snapshot is taken and the log is compacted. Audit segments and other digest-addressed content on replicas are immutable and keep their original encoding. h2s: Pros and cons of the options

blocking.section: Decision outcome (paragraph after the rules table)
blocking.issue: The ADR gives OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9 a scope that the owning document does not give it, and one of the two outcomes it names cannot be built. In the owning document, OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9 asks only about 'FIPS HTTP/3 given the quic-go G3 exception (golang/go#79219); G3 status of go-jose/v4, OPA, sigstore-go', with options '(a) HTTP/3 off in FIPS builds (current); (b) Ship with caveat'. It says nothing about how a FIPS Node treats `http3: true`. The 'validation error' outcome is not feasible as written. A Revision is rendered per Environment and has the same digest on FIPS and non-FIPS Nodes (pack section 8.1). `ruralz bundle validate`, `ruralz bundle build` and Ruralz Control validate the Bundle before any Node receives it, and they cannot know a target's build flavor, because no Configuration model field marks a Cluster or Environment as FIPS. The NACK outcome has a cost the ADR does not mention: a deterministic NACK fails the Rollout gate at once (pack section 8.3), so one FIPS Node in a mixed Cluster rolls back the Revision for every Node. The ADR also states a rule, 'it never ignores it', that no source owns.
blocking.evidence: "OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9 decides whether a FIPS Node answers a Revision with `http3: true` with a validation error or a NACK; it never ignores it."
blocking.fix: Replace the sentence with: "How a FIPS Node treats a Revision with `http3: true` is open. Ignoring the field would break equal behavior for equal digests (foundation pack section 8.1). A render-time error would need a field that marks FIPS targets, which the Configuration model lacks. A NACK fails the Rollout for a mixed Cluster. The owning document MUST add this case to OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9." Record the OQ-9 extension as an amendment to the owning document. Stay within the 1,200-word limit (the body is 1,195 words today) by using the savings from L1-3 and L1-4 or by shortening the Rust option's second Bad bullet.

blocking.section: Context and problem statement
blocking.issue: The ADR cites P1 as the authority for FIPS feature exclusions, but P1 says the opposite. Vision P1 says the product ships 'with one feature set in every public build, including the FIPS build', and Product non-goal 8 says every public build, including the FIPS build, 'has the same features (P1)'. The HTTP/3 exclusion actually comes from pack section 8.4, the Configuration model (Gateway) and the owning document (FIPS build). The hybrid post-quantum exclusion comes from the owning document only. A reader who follows the P1 link finds a principle that contradicts the sentence citing it.
blocking.evidence: "a FIPS build keeps the default build's license and features except the cryptography-bound exclusions, HTTP/3 and hybrid post-quantum key exchange (P1; OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9)"
blocking.fix: Change the citation to "(foundation pack section 8.4; [FIPS build](../engineering/01-tech-stack-and-libraries.md#fips-build); OQ-tech-stack-and-libraries-9)" and cite P1 only for the license: "a FIPS build keeps the default build's license (P1) and its features except ...". The foundation amendment reconciles P1 and pack section 1 with section 8.4.

blocking.section: Decision outcome > Consequences (CA roots bullet)
blocking.issue: The ADR names a library that has no catalog row, which foundation pack section 7 forbids: a design 'MUST NOT name a library until the tech stack document adds a catalog row backed by research'. The owning document also says 'A new direct dependency MUST get a catalog row in the same pull request'. The package sits under `golang.org/x/crypto`, so the G3 check as written ('fails on any `golang.org/x/crypto` package off the delegation allowlist') would reject it. No research URL backs it.
blocking.evidence: "or embedded through `golang.org/x/crypto/x509roots/fallback`, which has no catalog row or G3 allowlist entry."
blocking.fix: Replace the clause with: "or embedded in the binary, which needs a catalog row and a G3 decision that the owning document tracks as an Open question." Record that Open question as an amendment to the owning document.

blocking.section: Pros and cons of the options > Go with CGO enabled
blocking.issue: The ADR makes a performance claim that is untagged, unsupported and likely false. The research (go-libraries-runtime.md, lines 97 and 261) lists only the controls and says nothing about their cost. Fuel metering adds per-instruction accounting, and epoch interruption adds checks at function entries and loop back-edges. Both are cheaper than wazero's `WithCloseOnContextDone`, but neither is free. Style guide section 4 requires every performance figure to carry (target), (hypothesis) or a measurement URL, and this one has none.
blocking.evidence: "Good, because wasmtime offers fuel and epoch interruption with no per-loop cancellation cost ([source](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime-go/blob/main/config.go))."
blocking.fix: Rewrite as: "Good, because wasmtime offers fuel metering and epoch interruption, which wazero lacks, likely at lower cost than `WithCloseOnContextDone` (hypothesis) ([source](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime-go/blob/main/config.go))."

non_blocking.suggestion: Acceptance criterion 6 is not met yet: docs/adr/README.md does not exist. The owning document already links the ADR (Version floor, line 225). Confirm that the README index is produced in its later wave with an ADR-0001 row.

Add a Bad consequence (hypothesis) for the goroutine-per-connection model of `net/http`: idle WebSocket, SSE and Control Stream connections each hold a goroutine stack, which matters for the 96 MiB idle RSS budget (target). Name GOMEMLIMIT and GOGC, owned by Performance budgets and benchmarking, as the lever against the GC tail-latency risk.

non_blocking.section: Pros and cons of the options > Rust
non_blocking.suggestion: Drop wazero from the list of libraries 'no research file evaluates' in Rust, since research does evaluate wasmtime, a Rust runtime. Replace the stale-gateways bullet, which judges the language by two third-party products, with the real cost: a second toolchain and no shared validation library with Ruralz Control and the CLI. This also saves words for L1-1.

Say who names the FIPS build tag and where it is set (for example, the Makefile FIPS target owned by Repository layout and conventions). `GOFIPS140` does not add a build tag of its own; the Confirmation check that quic-go is absent from `go list -deps` would then catch a missing tag.
'images without a libc' describes image layout, which the ADR says belongs to Release, versioning and compatibility. Phrase it as what the language choice allows ('allows images without a libc').

blocking.issue: The non-Go gate applies the Go G2 allowlist unchanged to the Rust, npm and NuGet lockfiles. That allowlist is Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC and EDL-1.0 where elected. As written, the gate fails on the first Rust PDK build. A crate that uses serde derive locks `serde_derive -> syn -> proc-macro2 -> unicode-ident`. The `unicode-ident` license is '(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND Unicode-3.0', and Unicode-3.0 is not on G2. Other permissive licenses that are common in these ecosystems (Zlib, 0BSD, CC0-1.0, BlueOak-1.0.0) would fail the same way. Two things are also undefined. First, the gate does not say how an SPDX compound expression (OR/AND) is evaluated, while G2 handles dual licensing only by named election. Second, it does not say whether build-only dependencies count. Cargo.lock records proc-macro and build dependencies next to shipped ones, so 'production lockfile dependency' cannot be decided for Rust. The gate will either block every PDK pull request or be weakened ad hoc.

blocking.section: Decision outcome (Libraries row); Confirmation (Loader conformance suite)
blocking.issue: The ADR types substituted values by the YAML 1.2 core schema. The owning document instead has the rendered schema view re-type a whole-value expression, so the target field's type decides. The two rules differ in three buildable ways. (1) String fields: with `exact: ${CANARY}` and CANARY=true, or a label `version: ${APP_VERSION}` with APP_VERSION=1.10, core typing yields a boolean or the float 1.1, which fails RZ-CFG-005 or changes the value. Schema-directed typing keeps "true" and "1.10". (2) JSON files: every JSON string is double-quoted, so `"port": "${HTTPS_PORT}"` is never a plain scalar and never becomes an integer. The integer field then fails, which breaks the promise that `.json` files share the loader, schema and digest. (3) Flow-style YAML: `{` and `}` end a flow plain scalar, so authors must quote `"${VAR}"` there, and hit the same failure. The Confirmation encodes the wrong rule: 'substituted: `0777` MUST decode as decimal 777' is wrong for a string field, where the owning document keeps "0777". This item corrects the prior L1 fix, which proposed 'the same resolver re-types substituted values'. Raw plain scalars correctly stay under core-schema typing.
blocking.evidence: Line 53: "Ruralz types plain scalars from token text by the YAML 1.2 core schema (null, true/false, decimal, `0o` and `0x` integers, floats, else string), also after substitution, never by library typing." Line 104: "plain scalars `yes`, `on`, `0777`, `0b1`, `1_000` and `2026-09-23`, raw and substituted: `0777` MUST decode as decimal 777, the rest as strings." Configuration model, Environment substitution: "A value that is exactly one expression is re-typed by the rendered schema view (`port: ${HTTPS_PORT:-8443}` becomes an integer), while the authoring view accepts the unrendered string". Format decision: "`.json` files use the same loader and schema and yield the same Revision digest."
blocking.fix: Line 53: replace ", also after substitution, never by library typing." with ", never by library typing; a substituted whole-value expression, including a quoted or JSON one, takes the rendered view's type at its path." Line 104: replace "raw and substituted: `0777` MUST decode as decimal 777, the rest as strings." with "`0777` MUST decode as decimal 777 raw or substituted into an integer field, the rest as strings, and any value substituted into a string field MUST stay a string." The net change is about +14 words against a 1,192-word body. Offset it by cutting "; it stays an import source" (line 140), "; ambiguous features are rejected" (line 117), "Nothing is implemented yet." (line 23) and "; foundation pack section 7" (line 147).

blocking.section: Decision outcome (Restricted profile row); Consequences (second and fifth Bad bullets); Confirmation (Hostile input)
blocking.issue: Two parts of the ADR contradict each other. The Confirmation requires nesting fixtures that MUST fail with RZ-CFG-001. A Consequence says nesting depth stays unbounded. The decision table has no depth rule. As written, a nesting fixture either parses, which makes the gate fail, or overflows the stack. goccy/go-yaml's parser and the JSON Schema walk recurse per level, and roughly 32 million `[` characters fit in 64 MiB. A Go stack overflow past the 1 GB maximum is a fatal runtime error, not a recoverable panic, so it kills `ruralz-control` at ingest or a file-mode `ruralzd` watching a directory. The deferral cannot be traced. 'Open questions this ADR requests from the Configuration model' names no ID, and the Configuration model's Open questions table (OQ-configuration-model-2 to -17) has no depth or loader-memory question. An ADR is itself the section 14 change vehicle, so it can decide that a depth check exists and leave only the value open.
